#1058. Chelsea bullied by Brian Brobbey and Sunderland

Talk about cramming everything in. Brian Brobbey only played for 67 minutes but, in that time, he collected a yellow card, ripped Levi Colwill’s shirt and earned himself a standing ovation after morphing into a battering ram.

Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s head coach, said there was nobody like the Netherlands striker in the Premier League and it said everything that everyone wanted to make Brobbey centre of attention after a long overdue home win, even though he had not scored. Everyone, that is, bar Xabi Alonso.

“No, he’s not unstoppable,” Chelsea’s head coach replied when asked why his team had found Brobbey too much to handle. “He’s stoppable – but only when you defend better than we did. We were not bullied. We didn’t produce enough.”

That is one way of putting it. Another would be to say Brobbey was everything that Chelsea, much to Alonso’s disgust, were not: a bristling menace, a steamroller wearing a pair of boots, a player on a mission to help transform the mood – Enzo Le Fée’s decisive spot kick owed everything to Brobbey.

Chelsea arrived on Wearside looking to establish themselves in the top four ahead of the break but, instead, Alonso watched through his fingers as Sunderland reminded everyone why they were the joyous story of last season, a beautiful mix of inspiration and perspiration.

In fairness to the Chelsea manager, he refused to get caught in the minutiae of contentious penalty decisions – one that Chelsea were denied, another that they conceded – and could only lament as Sunderland ground out their first Premier League win since August 30, 70 long days ago.

“It wasn’t the best game,” Alonso said. “I think that we didn’t deserve more than probably one point, maybe. We need to be more consistent on the move, to get the ball from one side to the other, and we didn’t do that good enough. We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win.”

Unlike Sunderland. If you had turned up at the Stadium of Light without looking at the Premier League table, you would not have believed the hosts were bottom and you would not have given credence to the idea Le Bris, who has worked miracles these past two years, was under pressure.

Things, however, could not have started worse for Le Bris. Though Granit Xhaka has not shown last season’s form in these challenging opening months, the game plan was built around him, so to see the Sunderland captain hobbling off after three minutes was symptomatic of how things have gone for the Wearsiders.

“He felt something in the final sprint of the warm-up,” Le Bris explained. “We don’t know how bad it is.”

He is not the kind of coach, though, who will bemoan bad fortune. Le Bris sent on Jules Ahoka to replace Xhaka and watched as he, along with colleagues in red and white, set about trampling all over Chelsea’s intentions with incessant hard work.

Yet there was more to it. Sunderland can play, either intricately or directly, and a lovely move in the 12th minute needed a desperate, sliding intervention from Pep Chavarría’s to stop Trai Hume’s volley sliding in at the far post.

In the next attack, another Chemsdine Talbi cross – the Moroccan having been found by a peach of a pass from goalkeeper Robin Roefs – invited Brobbey to inflict maximum damage, but the Dutchman made a hash of his opportunity.

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The momentum could have changed completely in the 23rd minute. Alonso, his players and staff were convinced they would be given a penalty after Cole Palmer tumbled when his legs tangled with Luke O’Nien but, after a lengthy delay, VAR Nick Hopton felt there was no case to answer.

Hopton was involved again in the 33rd minute but, as Alonso said, Chelsea only had themselves to blame. Colwill simply could not contain Brobbey when he began marauding, grappling, grabbing and clipping the Dutchman’s heels. Le Fée did the rest, sending Mike Penders the wrong way.

Enzo Le Fee dispatches the penalty as Sunderland take the lead against Chelsea! 🔴⚪️ https://t.co/cCtYsHVWB9

From that point, Chelsea were in trouble, no matter how many changes Alonso made. They huffed, puffed, but nothing worked. They had come up against a red-and-white wall, fortified by constant backing from the stands, and the west Londoners were never going to knock it down.

One incident, as the clock ticked towards 90 minutes, encapsulated everything good about this Sunderland display when O’Nien chased down substitute Geovany Quenda to make a challenge. Another moment of defending from Thomas Meunier on Morgan Rogers was exceptional.

“You could see our identity and our togetherness and the way we managed the game,” said Le Bris, who was booked when hectoring referee Jarred Gillett. “These three points were critical. It was a struggle at times to manage situations. We showed as a group real heart.”

And nobody did that more than Brobbey. No wonder Le Bris will be hoping Xavi Hernández, the Netherlands head coach, handles him with care over the next 10 days. On this form, he will be the fuel that drives Sunderland’s quest for survival.

“You know when you come here in this stadium it will be a difficult game and that was the matter tonight. We knew it would be tough, we are disappointed we lost the game. At one point it went very fast from side to side. Sometimes we had to control. With 11 behind the ball it is difficult to find the spaces.”

On where Chelsea stand ahead of the international break...

“How you do – good or not – it is a matter of staying together. The international break is coming so the lads can be calm in the head and when we all come back we need to be motivated to go again.”

“For me it wasn’t a penalty. He barely touched him, I think it was the other way round. He grabbed him.”

They cannot make anything of set piece and Sunderland have the three points - it wasn’t pretty but they needed the three points and edged the contest.

Questions will be asked of Chelsea now, they were bullied in the first-half and weren’t able to create anything in the second.

Chelsea with the ball inside the Sunderland half. The visitors bring Rogers down and Chelsea have a free-kick. Last-chance sallon for the west Londoners...

Sunderland have a throw inside the Chelsea half - this is about game management for the side in dire need of a win now...

Angulo nrings down his man after a poor pass from Sadiki. The visitors with a free-kick inside their own half.

Emegha drifts past Mukiele before he feels the full force of a Luke O’Nein tackle. It looks as though he gets the ball but the ref awards the free-kick. It’s in the final third, can Chelsea create anything from this?

In short ‘yes’, Estevao delivers a peach of a ball and Welbeck gets on the end of it. BUT his header is over, when it seemed easier to hit the target.

Sunderland in Chelsea half, they’re looking for a free-kick as Angulo goes down. The referee isn’t having any of it...

Sunderland break at pace (only the second time this half) Isador finds Talbi who is free before cutting inside and unleashing a shot from outside the box. It’s just wide, don’t think it was too far away though.

Talbi is off for Angulo, Rigg on for Le Fee for Sunderland, and for Chelsea, Henderson makes way for Emegha.

For all their possession this half Chelsea have not forced Roefs into a meaningful save. The west Londoners are again dominating possession in and near the hinterland of the Sunderland box, but it’s all a bit after you Claude and ultimately Roefs gladly picks up an anaemic cross. That sums up Chelsea as an attacking force today.

Chelsea corner after Geovany Quenda gets in a shot from the left-side of the area that gets a tiny hint of a deflection. Roefs punches away the set-piece and Sunderland breathe a sigh of relief.

Better from Sunderland, there are spaces in behind Chelsea as the visitors go in search of the equaliser and over the past few minutes the hosts have found them.

Lovely ball from Reinildo finds Sadiki in space on the left, they keep the ball brilliantly before Le Fee plays in Isador, it’s a one-on-one and all the Frenchman has to do it dink it over the on-rushing keeper. He goes low, however, and Penders makes a fine save - that was the game for Sunderland there...Penders has kept Chelsea in this.

Brobbey may have been tiring but without him Sunderland cannot keep the ball. Sadiki earns a free-kick which takes a bit of pressure off the hosts.

Palmer pulls back for Gusto whose dinky, cheeky chip tries to find Roefs off his line. He doesn’t succeed and the Dutch goalkeeper claims with ease.

Chelsea still seeing plenty of the ball, Sunderland may well be tiring. It’s hard to keep up that intensity for 90 minutes, hence Isador on for Brobbey, but they are struggling to keep the ball at the moment.

The first half was lively and entertaining, this half has been lively and lacking in anything that could be remotely described as a spectacle...

Rogers tries to find Palmer, but the ball is too long and Roefs gobbles up with ease.

Meanwhile, Hume looks injured and Chelsea do not give the ball back after Sunderland kicked it off. You won’t be shocked to hear that the home fans are not happy with that...

Change for Sunderland, Brobbey off for Isador. The Dutchman has been brilliant today, he might have scored a couple of goals, but despite not finding the back of the net he has proved a handful for the Chelsea backline. I would have kept him on for longer...

Chelsea looking better this half, they’re seeing plenty of the ball but have not had a shot on goal since the break. In fact there have only been two touches in either box this 45...Sunderland won’t mind that at 1-0.

ON - Welbeck and GustoOFF - Neto and Palestra

So Alonso has opted for a physical presence up front.

No sooner had I pressed send on that last post than Chelsea break through the middle but some great last-ditch defending from Muenier prevents Estevao from getting a shot at goal.

Chelsea haven’t been able to play through Sunderland and you think they’d need to bring on a physical presence up front if that’s to change.

Another chance for Sunderland - they break down the right before Hume sends in a low ball to the penalty box, it’s met first time by Le Fee, I think, and Penders saves low to his right. To state the obvious, the hosts would love a second to give them a deserved cushion. As I typed that last but the linesman has his flag up, it wouldn’t have counted, promising signs nonetheless.

Pressure from Sunderland. A good bit of possession ends with Mukiele swinging in a lovely cross from the right which Chelsea are forced to head clear for a corner. Nothing results from the set piece, but things still looking promising for Sunderland who look as energetic and ‘at it’ as they did in the first half.

Rogers picks up the ball in the middle just inside the Sunderland half and is immediately pick-pocketed by one of three Sunderland players. The Chelsea men have not been allowed to settle when they have a sniff of a mini counter.

Good, feisty opening to this half, Chelsea look more up for it, though to be fair they couldn’t look any more insipid than they did in the first 45. Meanwhile, Brobbey shoves Lavia and earns a yellow. Think that’s three yellows for the hosts now.

It is going to be fascinating to see how a team with well known - and long standing - disciplinary issues copes with a pressurised pursuit of an equaliser. There have already been a couple of flash points that Chelsea’s players have reacted to and it wouldn’t be the wildest thing to predict referee Jarred Gillett brandishing a red card before the end of the game. Watch it unfold with interest.

Brobbey lays the ball off for Meunier in the final third, it’s asking a lot of the Belgian but his compounds the Dutchman’s error with one of his own - stretching for the ball and taking out Caicedo. Something for which he earns a needless yellow card.

There’s a bit of argy bargy on the pitch, not sure what started that but the referee Jarred Gillett has to have a word with several players. All a bit of handbags really.

They’re back under way on the banks of the Wear. Chelsea have been insipid and you imagine they won’t be as bed these next 45 minutes. Can Sunderland play with the same aggression and energy? We’re about to find out.

Changes Estevao on for Colwill, interesting substitution to say the least...

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The half ends with an audacious attempt at goal from Rogers, a full 40 yards out from a free kick. It’s catching practice for Roefs and that sums up Chelsea as an attacking force in the first 45. Sunderland are well worth their lead.

Rogers has a shot-cum-cross from the left and it sails high, wide and not so handsome. He’s been on the periphery this half, as has Palmer and that explains as much as anything why they are behind. Sunderland have cut out the supply to him and Roefs has had little to do as a result.

Approaching half-time and save for the contentious VAR call when he wanted a penalty, Cole Palmer has done absolutely nothing. The talk of him being in the England squad, on this evidence, is for the birds. Sunderland are full value for their half-time lead. Chelsea, like Palmer, have been absolutely insipid.

There will be five minutes added time in this first half.

Something I’ve not written much this half ‘chance for Chelsea’. Neto works a bit of space in the inside-right channel outside the box, but his shot is easily saved by Roefs.

Talbi attacks down the left but cuts in when he would have been better served going wide.

Chelsea have seen plenty of the ball but they’ve been way too slow and cumbersome with it. It’s been in front of the Sunderland back lines and easy to defend against. The hosts are letting the visitors have the ball wide and with Neto in the middle, it’s been too easy for Le Bris’s men.

Brobbey wants the ball at every opportunity and Sunderland would be well advised to give it to him. Colwill is has his hands full.

Sunderland have kept the aggression and energy throughout the half - and kept Chelsea quiet as a result. As I type that the hosts give Lavia too much room 25 yards out and his shot is well wide of the left-hand post.

The lead is no more than Sunderland deserve and that means, as the table stands, Manchester United are bottom of the Premier League. Fair play to Enzo Le Fee for keeping his nerve in a pressure situation. Sunderland needed him to be cool.

They’ve deserved that, they’ve been the better side and are well worth the lead. Le Fee sends Penders the wrong way, burying the ball into the bottom left corner.

Brobbey has been a handful (as he always is) and Colwill brings the BIG (yes, caps lock and bold are necessary) Dutchman down in the box. It looks as though it was six of one and hald a dozen of the other, but the spotkick stands.

Ahoka has impressed since coming on, his nifty footwork helps win Sunderland a throw in the final third. Mukiele has a big thrown on him but it does not result in a chance. Still, this is good from the hosts and Chelsea are second best at the moment. They were in the first half against United last week, and ended up winning so...

Another chance for Sunderland as Brobbey bullies Colwill on the halfway line before driving at Fofana. He gets to the edge of the area, beats the Chelsea defender before his shot goes wide. The last touch took him too wide, but again, promising signs for the hosts.

Early days this, of course, but Sunderland absolutely do not look like a team that is currently the worst in the Premier League. They should have the lead here but Brian Brobbey’s miss from six yards is indicative of how things have been going.

Sunderland are being aggressive, they need to be and it’s a contrast from the previous month. With that approach, however, comes risks and Mukiele gives away a free-kick inside his own half. Luckily for him, nothing comes from the set-piece.

First chance of the game for Chelsea and, as with Brobbey 10 minutes ago, it should have found the back of the net. Rogers is the culprit - he sends his header wide of the right post after a grade-A cross from Palestra.

One-all in terms of great chances...but the score remains 0-0.

Palmer is bundled over on the outskirts of the area and he and Chelsea players appeal for something - could be a free-kick of penalty...the referee is having nothing of it. The replay suggests he may well have been hard done by but VAR also is having nothing of it...it was a foul as none of the marauding Sunderland players, O’Nien among them (obviously), got the ball and most definitely got Palmer...think the hosts got away with that one.

Yellow card for Ahoka for a foul on Caicado, he may need to walk a tightrope for the rest of the match. But it’s an illustration of the energy and purpose with which Sunderland have approached this match.

Sunderland have looked the better side so far and have had the better chances.

Better from Chelsea in the sense that they controlled the game for two minutes. Lots of good, neat passing but no end product, it’s all in front of a composed Sunderland defence.

Another good chance for Sunderland and once again Talbi proves his worth. He cuts back onto his right and delivers a peach of a cross from the left. Brobbey gets in front of his man and all he has to do is hit the target...alas his first-time shot goes wide. That should be 1-0 to the hosts who are the better side at the moment.

Good from Sunderland who look so much more energetic than at any point during their previous few matches. Ahoka does well in the middle before freeing Talbi down the left. The Moroccan gets in a cross and Le Fee’s shot is blocked. Promising signs for the hosts.

What a blow this is for Regis Le Bris. Less than two minutes gone and Granit Xhaka is having to leave the pitch with an obvious injury. Some fans around the press box booed Xhaka as he was hobbling off - is that a hangover from his attempts to move to Chelsea? - but on afternoon when Le Bris needed everything to go his way, he’s already on the back foot.

Neto is in the Sunderland half but three Sunderland players snap at his heels like a hyperactive dog after a bone. Chelsea haven’t been allowed to settle yet. Plenty of time to go though...

Sunderland are looking to find Brobbey at every opportunity, but Chelsea’s backline intercept well. Nothing of note created so far, but the hosts are on the front foot, which is what they and the fans needed.

Sunderland attack down the right with Meunier, nothing comes of it but the hosts look as though they mean business here. A minute later Sadiki and Brobbey nearly combine to create something. Close but no cigar...

Bad news for Sunderland, Xhaka is down and it looks as though he may well have to come off...oh dear. While he’s not been at his best this season he’s still the man the side looks towards for inspiration (an boy do they need that is dollops today...)...and, indeed he is forced off. Ahoka, who is highly rated but raw replaces him. The Congolese player now has a big chance to make a name for himself.

Chelsea with the early possession, but they go backwards and the hosts are up and at them with the press and the visitors have to go back to Penders in goal.

They’re under way at the Stadium of Light, Sunderland are in their famous red and white and Chelsea in their away outfit of black shirts and shorts and yelow socks.

As the Stadium of Light remembers all those who lost their lives in war.

The Last Post is played and the minute’s silence is impeccably observed.

Warming-up in our Remembrance shirt ❤️ https://t.co/aTB8sfdLKP

And we’re moments away from kick-off in the North East.

This is a big afternoon for both teams. It will be an emotional one, too, for Jordan Henderson, who started his career at Sunderland many years ago. Xabi Alonso has confirmed he has been picked because of the quality he provides, rather than any sentimental value, and Regis Le Bris revealed ahead of the fixture he tried to bring the England international home during the summer window, when Chelsea attempted to sign Granit Xhaka.

“Jordan is a great player, first of all,” said Le Bris. “For the connection with the club, it’s not my part. It was with Flo [Ghisolfi, director of football] and Kyril [Louis-Dreyfus, the Sunderland owner], they had conversations.

“I thought that it could have been a good signing for the club, a good symbol, a great player, a great leader. But the market is the market.”

Has just said that Sunderland, and in particular Brian Brobbey, can ‘get at’ the Chelsea defence of Palestra, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria. I am not sure he has seen much of the Sunderland attack this year, but Brobbey is a handful for any defence.

“We have to stay consistent and true to our identity. It’s always difficult to predict what the other side does but you have to focus on yourself and connect with the fans and impose our ideas.”

On whether they can get a result today...

“I hope so... I see the players every day, they care and sometime its hard to understand the unforced errors.”

“He’s loved by fans and team, so we know the situation at beginning of season. He is an important player for us and didn’t start for various reasons, but has qualities run in behind and finish - he’s excited worked and has worked hard.”

I mentioned earlier that Sunderland did the double over Chelsea last season. But the manner of the victories revealed more than the scorelines. In both matches, especially the second, the west Londoners looked somewhat lightweight and easily bullied.

This season Xabi Alonso has been determined to ensure that that is not the case this season.

In the land of the Premier League giants, Chelsea have been on the small side in recent seasons. But they are no longer being looked down upon and are finally showing signs of being capable of going toe-to-toe physically with opponents.

Sunday’s opponents Sunderland ran Chelsea off the park twice last season. Only once, in the 36th Premier League game of the campaign against Liverpool, did Chelsea cover more distance than their opposition.

Here’s Matt Law’s article on Why Chelsea have gone from pint-sized players to taller trees...

SUNDERLAND XI TO FACE CHELSEA: Roefs, Meunier, Mukiele, O’Nein, Reinildo, Xhaka, Hume, Le Fee, Talbi, Brobbey.

Subs: Ellborg, Danso, Methalie, Rigg, Tutierov, Ahoka, Fofana, Angulo, Isador

Regis Le Bris makes two changes from the sorry defeat at Coventry City. Nordi Mukiele returns to the centre of defence and there’s a start for Chemsdine Talbi  – Chris Rigg and Nilson Angulo are the ones to make way.

CHELSEA XI TO FACE SUNDERLAND: Penders, Palestra, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria, Henderson, Lavia, Caicedo, Neto, Palmer, Rogers.

Subs: Sharman-Lowe, Gusto, Anselmino, Nicoll-Jazuli, Barco, Quenda, Estevao, Welbeck, Emegha.

Xabi Alonso also makes two changes – Pep Chavarria and Jordan Henderson start today. Estevao Willian drops to the bench while Josh Acheampong is a somewhat surprise absence the 20.

Goalkeeper Mike Penders continues in goal with Emiliano Martinez deemed not ready to return having fractured his jaw against Everton.

That Sunderland did the double over Chelsea last season.

A last-minute winner from Chemsdine Talbi grabbed the points at Stamford Bridge, before Sunderland won 2-1, without breaking sweat, at the Stadium of Light on the last day of the campaign.

Those victories, and the manner of them, underlined what a season it was for Regis Le Bris’s men. How they wish this campaign started as that one ended.

RLB's XI to take on Chelsea! 📝👊 #SUNCHE https://t.co/1XWyHk0x56

Your Chelsea side today! ✔️ #CFC | #SUNCHE https://t.co/ciaILJeAuu

For Sunderland that argument is easy to make – they are bottom of the Premier League, are without a win since August and for morale, if nothing else need at least a point, though three is really what the doctor orders.

For Chelsea – fourth in the table and with three wins in their past four league outings – the argument that this is a must-win game is harder to make, but bear with me here...

Facing a Sunderland team who are suffering from the worst of both worlds – blunt in attack and pitiful in defence (what a difference from last season...) and have proven all too easy to beat (as their 2-0 home defeat Zagreb illustrated on Thursday) – the west Londoners are expected to win. Fail to return to the capital with the three points and there will once again be question marks over Xabi Alonso’s side. They are flaky and flashy in equal measure, able to play and win well in spurts, but once again unable to mount sustained pressure needed for a title challenge and forced to battle it out for the hope of a top-four spot at best. Those will be the arguments raised should they not win this afternoon.

The hosts doubtless wish that their ‘issues’ were as golden as today’s opposition. For Trai Hume, who scored in this fixture last season, the Sunderland players are at fault for the sorry start to the season and he wants to put right the wrongs so far, starting today.

“I couldn’t tell you what’s changed. We thought we’d addressed it after the Leeds game, where we were aggressive, strong, but we go out there tonight and see the old habits of the start of the season. Everything’s a bit laboured, and it’s something the staff can’t fix, it’s on us as players,” Hume said.

“We’re still together as a club, as a team. I think the run of form we’re on, it would be easy to think we’re not, but we are. We are really upset with how we’ve been playing, and the results don’t lie. We haven’t been good enough and we know that. We have to address that.”

#1057. Football fan arrest numbers branded ‘unacceptable’ by policing chief

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Police praised supporters who travelled to North America for their conduct but warned that wider football-related disorder remains a concern

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Latest arrest figures for fans watching last summer’s World Cup are "unacceptably" high despite excluding linked crimes such as domestic abuse, football’s policing lead has said.

Home Office data shows 357 arrests occurred in England and Wales linked to fans watching England matches during the North American tournament, compared to just 19 arrests at the event itself.

Chief Constable Mark Hobrough, National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) lead for football policing, praised travelling fans for "exemplary" behaviour, but described conduct at home during the World Cup and 2025-26 domestic season as far more troubling.

He said: "Though the vast majority of supporters attending domestic fixtures in the UK are law-abiding and enjoy supporting their teams at great games, there still remain an unacceptable number who spoil the event for others.

"2,025 people were arrested for football-related incidents during the domestic season in 2025-26, and disappointingly this number is up from 2,004 in 2024-25.

"In addition, 357 people were arrested in England and Wales for football-related incidents during the 2026 World Cup alone.

"Sadly, these figures do not paint a full picture as they do not include many of the associated offences, such as domestic abuse, which often occur behind closed doors after the full-time whistle has blown and in many cases nowhere near any stadium or club with individuals who’ve not attended any game themselves.

"However, as the figures show, we are continuing to take action against those responsible, and moving forward, we will continue to work with our partners including the Crown Prosecution Service, the Premier League, the EFL and the Football Association to collectively make football a safe environment for the overwhelming majority of supporters who just want to enjoy the game."

Home Office figures for 2025-26, first released in July showing 1,963 football-related arrests or police actions, have now been revised to 2,025.

Total arrests across the 2025-26 season—including domestic games, the World Cup, and European fixtures abroad—reached 2,403, falling from 2,584 in 2023-24, the previous men’s tournament season.

Tournament-related arrests within England and Wales increased compared to 2023-24, a change the Home Office attributed to better recording and awareness among police forces.

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has an uncertain future at Old Trafford

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United could be about to land Jobe Bellingham as their long-term replacement for Bruno Fernandes.

The Red Devils' poor start to the season has been punctuated by the uncertainty surrounding their captain, with Fernandes having fallen out with manager Michael Carrick earlier this season.

Looking to a future beyond the 32-year-old, recent England call-up Bellingham has now emerged as a potential option in the middle for Manchester United.

Fernandes was dropped by Carrick for the match against Bournemouth, following comments made after the Red Devils' 4-1 humbling by Como in the Champions League.

United fans sang Carrick's name after the loss to the Cherries, however, and booed the players – with Fernandes making up with the manager and returning to the starting line-up ever since.

Yet according to Fichajes, the Portuguese is still a target for Atletico Madrid, as they look to take advantage of the situation.

The report names Bellingham as a “gamble” that the club could well take to replace their talismanic playmaker, with the 21-year-old thriving at Borussia Dortmund, just as brother Jude did previously.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Jobe has recently been named in Thomas Tuchel's England squad for the November internationals alongside his elder sibling, who he shares a similar profile with.

Despite Fichajes noting that “there is no evidence of an offer from United” just yet, however, the Red Devils were heavily invested in Jude Bellingham when he was on the move and could well take a similar interest in Jobe.

United offered £30 million for Jude when he was a Birmingham City youngster, as per Sky Sports, only for the player himself to choose the Bundesliga for his own development.

Jobe has had a similar path, moving from Birmingham to Sunderland before making the switch to Signal Iduna Park at the start of last season.

Bellingham is worth €40 million, according to Transfermarkt. Manchester United travel away to Liverpool when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

#1055. Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Climate change is affecting many types of crop, including these unusually small potatoes.Credit: John Thys/AFP/Getty

Policymakers at the United Nations COP31 climate conference that started this week in Antalya, Turkey, will know that the UN Environment Programme has confirmed that global warming will exceed the limit of 1.5 °C above pre-industrial temperatures agreed in 2015 in Paris. This meeting comes hot on the heels of the UN COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, which affirmed yet again that the world is also in the middle of a biodiversity crisis. Progress in each case, whether preventing dangerous climate change or stemming biodiversity loss, is too slow. But researchers across scientific disciplines are now arguing that advances in biotechnology could provide solutions1. Methods such as gene editing and germplasm mining — the analysis of huge libraries of plant-genome sequences to find useful traits for crop improvement — can now be used to tackle global warming and protect nature, scientists write in a climate-themed issue of Nature Biotechnology.

There was a time — not that long ago — when many considered biotechnologies a threat to the environment. But as the special issue shows, a shift is under way. Now, the field offers strategies for protecting both climate and biodiversity from the many damaging effects of industrial agriculture.

To feed a growing global population, between 2015 and 2024, the amount of cultivated land grew by roughly eight million hectares a year1. Yet, if the greenhouse-gas emissions, and thus global warming, this expansion causes is to be avoided, the world must work out how to produce enough food within its current agricultural footprint. Land clearance and land-use change contributes up to five billion tonnes of carbon annually — and is a major cause of biodiversity loss. Here, biotech solutions have some of the greatest potential, for example, by helping to increase crop yields and to protect plants from heat, drought and disease.

How biotechnology can mitigate climate change by curbing the global land squeeze

How biotechnology can mitigate climate change by curbing the global land squeeze

Of 77 such technologies with applications in agriculture, aquaculture and other sectors, many are ready for large-scale testing in the field, propose bioengineers Shekhar Mishra, Lauren Lui and Adam Arkin at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California in a Perspective article2. Argentina, China and the United States have given the green light to engineered drought-tolerant crops.

Rice farming produces around 9% of human-caused emissions of the greenhouse gas methane. Now, researchers have found a way to slash these emissions, write agronomist Yunkai Jin at Hunan Agricultural University in Changsha, China, and his colleagues in a Comment article3.

But technological readiness isn’t enough: governments, regulators and the public need to be ready, too4. Readers might have a sense of déjà vu: in the 1990s, advances in biotechnology promised a revolution in food and agriculture — which subsequently stalled. The ambition was to genetically modify crops or engineer them in other ways so that they could tolerate herbicides, resist insects and fight viruses. But, at the time, many scientists, governments and corporations promoting the technology gave insufficient attention to several issues.

Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture

Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture

One concern was public anxiety about the idea of eating food produced using transgenic technologies — crops modified by inserting a gene from another plant species or other organism. Another issue was that risks to the environment and to human health had not been studied sufficiently. A third problem was that multinational companies dominated both the research and the development of these technologies, creating fears that the rise of agricultural biotechnology would put many small family farms out of business.

Environmental groups found common cause with consumer organizations. Together, they urged governments to enact strict regulations. In the European Union, for example, risks to human health and the environment needed to be assessed before technologies producing genetically modified organisms could be commercialized. Although this was necessary, it slowed down advances in low- and middle-income countries, because any nation intending to export produce to the EU would have to prove that it was not genetically modified.

Since then, at least two things have changed, increasing optimism about the use of biotechnology to help the planet. The discovery of gene editing — in which an organism’s genes are modified precisely to produce specific traits — has proved transformational for agriculture. The method is being developed cautiously and is regulated in a more nuanced way than were conventional technologies that produce genetically modified crops. In June, the EU amended its regulations on genetic modification and now permits the cultivation of some gene-edited crops.

Low-methane rice is near — the world should deploy it

Low-methane rice is near — the world should deploy it

A second development is that catastrophic events such as heatwaves and floods have meant that climate change and the planet’s protection have become mainstream concerns across science and society, not just for environmental research. In a way, we all need to be environmentalists now, and this provides a rationale for governments to reconsider adopting biotech solutions with appropriate safeguards in place.

Advances in biotechnology that limit land use should be deployed to slow down the rise in global temperatures and biodiversity loss. This will require a partnership between the private sector, scientists, conservationists and farmers. High-yielding crops produced using industrial agriculture have helped to feed the world but have also had a devastating effect on biodiversity. Organic agriculture is more sustainable but requires extra land, because its yields tend to be lower than those from industrial methods. Providing they are implemented wisely, safely and ethically, biotechnologies could contribute to innovative farming methods that offer the best of both worlds.

#1054. Man United Supporters’ Trust underlines ‘depressing moment’ after Michael Carrick sacked

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The supporters’ group said “responsibility for United’s problems... lie with the ownership” rather than Carrick

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The Manchester United Supporters’ Trust (MUST) has branded Michael Carrick’s sacking “another depressing moment” and argued the club’s problems rest primarily with its ownership, in a now-familiar plea to end the ongoing feeling of crisis at Old Trafford.

United sacked Carrick just 10 games into the Premier League season with the club in the relegation zone and having won just once in this domestic campaign.

The club’s hierarchy met minority owner Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco on Wednesday to discuss Carrick’s future and a statement on Thursday said that it had “come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions”.

Former Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea manager Mauricio Pochettino, who currently manages the US men’s national team, is in line to replace him.

The club statement paid tribute to former midfielder Carrick as a “Manchester United legend” and the MUST statement concurred, saying “his standing among supporters remains undiminished”, but criticised the ownership for the spiral the club has found itself in.

It said: “Michael Carrick’s departure marks another depressing moment for Manchester United. We thank him for his service and for restoring hope during the second half of last season. His standing among supporters remains undiminished.

“The reason Manchester United fans have continued to support Michael Carrick in recent weeks is that they know that responsibility for United’s problems do not primarily rest with him or indeed his predecessors as manager. They lie with the ownership.

“The Glazers’ debt-funded takeover continues to burden the club. When Ineos came in they promised sporting excellence, but yet with repeated changes in football leadership we have seen anything but.

“It is time for the owners to explain themselves and show some accountability.”

MUST continued to criticise “aggressive ticketing policies” which “have further damaged relations with supporters”, arguing “supporters are being asked to pay the price for the owners’ mismanagement as well as their stadium ambitions through higher charges and diminished rights”.

It continued: “The unprecedented scale of the booing at Old Trafford, alongside public criticism from senior players in recent weeks, now points to a deeper deterioration. These are signs of a club becoming more divided, with the bond between supporters, players and those running Manchester United under increasing strain.”

Defender Lisandro Martinez criticised the club’s hierarchy for not doing more to support Carrick in the transfer market following the 2-1 Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid last month, while dire on-pitch performances have resulted in protests against the ownership and loud booing of the players, although there were public displays of support for Carrick by fans at Old Trafford.

MUST concluded: “The owners must allow senior club management to change direction: show accountability, rebuild trust, listen to supporters and recognise that their loyalty is fundamental to football success.

“Another change of head coach cannot repair what the ownership continues to undermine.”

Liverpool are planning their long-term future in goal, with the Brighton stopper linked

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Liverpool are looking to Bart Verbruggen of Brighton & Hove Albion as their successor in goal to Alisson.

Verbruggen has been in spectacular form for the high-flying Seagulls this season, keeping seven clean sheets in 10 Premier League appearances, with the Sussex outfit finding themselves second in the table – four points ahead of Liverpool.

Such good form means increased interest in some of Brighton's top performers, however, with the Reds turning attentions to the Amex.

Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson is out of contract at the end of the season, with his imperiously high level having perhaps dropped this season with age.

The Brazilian is now 34 and has made a couple of high-profile errors this season – while his comments admitting that he missed Liverpool matches last season “to prepare for the World Cup” have not gone down well with fans.

Now, TEAMtalk have revealed in a report that the Merseysiders have begun to look to the future between the sticks and have identified Verbruggen as a “credible candidate who could provide stability and quality” in taking the No.1 shirt at Anfield.

Alisson was a transformational signing for previous manager Jurgen Klopp in the wake of Loris Karius' two mistakes in the 2018 Champions League final, establishing himself as arguably the best goalkeeper in the Premier League since joining the Reds from Roma on what was an all-time record for a keeper at the time.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Liverpool looked to future-proof the position in 2025 when they swooped for highly-rated Georgian, Giorgi Mamardashvili, but the 26-year-old has struggled to command the same kind of aura as Alisson.

Next summer, manager Andoni Iraola will welcome 18-year-old Lucca Brughmans from Belgian side Genk in a move that could rise to an impressive £30 million – but a need remains for a senior figure to replace their current first-choice in goal.

Verbruggen is said to be happy at Brighton, though there is interest in his services from Real Madrid, too, who are looking to life beyond Thibaut Courtois themselves.

Manager Fabian Hurzeler will not entertain offers for the Dutchman in January, according to the report, with the player himself reiterating that he is fully focused on life on the south coast.

“I don’t know what will happen in the future: no one knows,” Verbruggen stated recently, adding, “All I know is that, at the moment, I’m very happy in Brighton.”

The Seagulls stopper is worth €40 million, according to Transfermarkt. Liverpool face Manchester United when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

Bosnia-Herzegovina is evolving as a footballing nation, relying on the pull of emotional ties and homeland pride to spearhead their upcoming qualification campaigns

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Following the retirement of long-time talisman Edin Dzeko, Bosnia-Herzegovina is undergoing a generational shift. Largely, and somewhat uniquely, it is being powered by the emotional pull of a vast global diaspora.

With the domestic league severely underfunded and ill-equipped to serve as a reliable talent conveyor belt for the national team, looking beyond its borders has become a necessity. A series of gifted foreign-born prospects, eligible for their countries of birth yet choosing instead to represent their heritage, is reshaping the team's identity.

At the heart of this recruitment drive is former captain turned sporting director Emir Spahic, who framed the philosophy in late 2024 with a simple declaration: “We’re just bringing our children home.” Having already fielded the third-youngest squad at the 2026 World Cup, this borderless strategy is no longer a temporary stopgap but the blueprint for the nation's footballing future.

A product of Bayer Leverkusen’s academy, Kerim Alajbegovic had a tremendously successful season at Red Bull Salzburg in 2025/2026, registering 14 goals and four assists in 44 competitive appearances in his first season of senior football.

Largely operating on the left flank, Alajbegovic is exceptional in 1-v-1 situations, and is comfortable with both feet. He has begun to hone his game in dead ball situations, developing a signature in-swinging technique on corners from the left, too.

What is striking for a player who only turned 19 in September is that Alajbegovic exudes the confidence of someone who has spent many years playing at the top level, and does not seem phased by the challenges that lie ahead.

His spectacular solo goal against Qatar in Bosnia-Herzegovina’s final group game made him the eighth youngest goalscorer at a World Cup, and the youngest-ever to score from outside the box.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Though Bayer Leverkusen had activated a buy-back clause from Red Bull Salzburg before the tournament, he garnered interest from several top European clubs, before signing for Juventus.

Alajbegovic told Tuttosport that speaking to Miralem Pjanic, a national team legend who spent four trophy-laden seasons in Turin, was an influential factor in his decision.

Alajbegovic’s accomplishments this year were recognised with a place at the Ballon d’Or ceremony, where he was voted 7th in the Men’s Young Talent of the Year award.

Born in Wisconsin in 2005, Esmir Bajraktarevic grew up in a Bosnian household but moved up through the ranks of the game in the USA, establishing himself at New England Revolution in MLS.

After representing the USA at youth level, and gaining one cap at senior level, Bajraktarevic switched to Bosnia-Herzegovina. As a child, he idolised Edin Dzeko, and earlier this year a video of a five-year-old Bajraktarevic wearing a Dzeko top kicking a ball in his back garden went viral. On his international debut against the Netherlands in September 2024, Bajraktarevic set up his boyhood hero with a signature lofted through-ball, and his cinematic rise in the national team was capped off by scoring the deciding penalty kick against Italy to secure Bosnia-Herzegovina’s World Cup qualification.

Bajraktarevic is a left-footed winger operating on the right, who possesses excellent close control and the ability to carve open defences with pinpoint crosses. On his day, he is an electrifying player to watch, whose body feints and mesmerising dinks bring fans out of their seats. Since his move to PSV Eindhoven in January 2025, game-time has sometimes been hard to come by, but this season he has seven goal contributions to his name despite only having 384 Eredivisie minutes under his belt.

Mahmic’s inclusion in Bosnia-Herzegovina’s World Cup squad came as a surprise, given that his impressive performances at Slovan Liberec had gone under the radar in the national media, and he was yet to be capped at senior level.

But the 21-year-old rose to the occasion, scoring a thunderous volley two minutes into his competitive debut versus Switzerland in Los Angeles, before scoring the goal against Qatar that confirmed Bosnia-Herzegovina’s place in the knockout stages of the World Cup. Most frequently deployed in a traditional No. 10 role, Mahmic’s best attributes include his ability to shoot from range and his passing vision, but he also has a knack for popping up in the box to score goals. At six feet tall, Mahmic’s frame enables him to protect the ball effectively when trying to pick out his teammates, too.

On the back of his eye-catching World Cup performances, Mahmic was signed by Corum, an ambitious, newly-promoted club in the Turkish Super Lig, for the second-highest transfer fee in the club’s history. He then scored on his debut against Besiktas and contributed regularly in the final third despite limited time on the pitch.

#1051. Destiny brought Mauricio Pochettino to Man United - but one huge question remains

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Argentine has come close to becoming Manchester United manager on three separate prior occasions. Now the stars appear to have finally aligned, but is it too late for either the man or the club?

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

On Sunday evening, Mauricio Pochettino got the call he had been waiting for.

He and long-time assistant Jesus Perez had frequently asked about Manchester United over the last decade. They would often contact friends in the game who were connected to Old Trafford, looking to find out what was happening, whether there could be an opening.

Pochettino came very close to taking one of those openings on at least three occasions: 2018, 2021 and 2024. Now, elements might finally have aligned.

It is a call that others at Old Trafford have long waited for, too. Back when they had a much publicised dinner in 2016, Sir Alex Ferguson essentially told Pochettino he should be the United manager. The Argentine was enthralled at that meeting by stories from one of the game’s great glory eras, and a sense of magic he had felt just standing in Old Trafford had been deepened.

Pochettino had been especially taken by Ferguson’s account of rebuilding United from the 1980s, initially drawing comparisons with what he was doing at Tottenham Hotspur. Now, he’s set to take on that exact same job, if one that has become so much bigger than in 2016. It is arguably even bigger than in 1986.

Pochettino, however, is fired by the idea of being the man to finally fix United. It has become one of the great managerial quests. The United hierarchy have ultimately gone for him because of that personality, and his standing. They don’t want a coach who hasn’t worked at this level. They want someone ready. Both the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe can sense that, since the two sides of the United ownership have known Pochettino for years.

If this is an appointment that always felt destined, though, that does raise one big question. Is this the right moment for it? Is it like Jose Mourinho, in that it came too late? Is it typical of modern United in that sense? Is it the same old “magical thinking” of hoping a famous name saves them, when the game has changed and the actual problems are now so structural?

Pochettino probably should have gone to United in 2016 or 2018, when he was at a peak in terms of being one of the most exciting coaches in football. The club did consider a move in the summer of 2016, but sources say an exit clause was allowed to expire. How different things could have been.

Old Trafford insiders are now talking about the value of “a name”, but the hierarchy did pass on Pochettino in 2024, when they initially considered sacking Erik ten Hag before ultimately deciding to stick with the Dutchman. His interview wasn’t seen as convincing as that of Thomas Tuchel or Roberto De Zerbi. Those who know him also say he is closer to being “a manager” now, in terms of a wider outlook, rather than the on-the-grass coach that so drove Spurs.

The very fact United are negotiating to pry him from the United States national team, without wishing to be disrespectful, also illustrates how his stock has recently dropped. Some close to Pochettino would nevertheless put that down to necessary choices at certain moments. Taking charge of the hosts of the biggest World Cup ever, that had so much pomp around it, was too enticing. Before that, he probably should have pushed to go to United or Real Madrid in 2018 but he was convinced he could do something special with Spurs. He’d put too much into it.

And that does point to one of the other great twists of fate in modern football, where Pochettino’s profile could be completely different. His Tottenham team were genuinely one of the best in Europe over 2016-18, and one of the great Premier League teams. To achieve 86 points in 2016-17, on what was then only the sixth highest wage bill in English football, was genuine alchemy. It was immense overperformance, fostered by a side that could just overrun you.

We also now know that the wage bill of the eventual champions for that season, Chelsea, had in part come from signings that had been secured by payments against the rules. The punishment from that guilty verdict still looks weak. There is a strong argument that Chelsea should have been stripped of the 2015 and 2017 titles. Pochettino himself said as much in a wide-ranging interview with The Independent and other media in September: “I’ve said that, that we should win one title, one Premier League. We should have been awarded it… for sure, we deserve to be champions for that year.”

Had that justice been done, Pochettino would not just be a “name” who created an exciting Spurs once. He would be an English champion, and one responsible for one of the most historic titles given the much wealthier competition. A great institution would have won just their third title, and first in 56 years.

Both he and Spurs could have had their futures transformed, as well as their place in history. It would have been a modern equivalent of what Ferguson himself did with Aberdeen.

Now, he wants to follow Ferguson in a different way. This is the job he has been waiting for.

A certain apathy towards the US job was displayed in that September interview when he spoke about how his contract didn’t necessarily mean he’d stay the full term.

For all of that, and how their World Cup campaign ended in the chaos of Donald Trump’s disruptive interference in the Falorin Balogun case, there were very impressive spells when the US really looked like a classic Pochettino team. The way they ripped into Paraguay was reminiscent of Spurs 2016-18, right up to some of the flourishes. And that was in a much more limited and restricted environment than a club team.

This is the other thing about just taking the job, too. Regardless of United’s current problems, and perceptions of where Pochettino is in his career, he is energised by this. He has that bite. As one figure who knows him well says, “he has got the IP, he has got the brand, he has got the experience”.

Having already worked for Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain, he’s been at big clubs with demanding owners. He has the mettle for that. And he now looks set to have the big job he’s always wanted.

#1050. Man Utd are in relegation trouble and Carrick must be sacked

Michael Carrick stood perfectly still and raised his left arm, and his index finger, high in the air. Around him, chaos. As it had been all afternoon. Substitute Patrick Dorgu had just headed in a corner to rescue a point for Manchester United in the 96th minute and, maybe, save Carrick his job.

Going into added time and United were two goals behind. It seemed all was lost for them against Aston Villa and for their head coach, but how telling was the reaction, in the directors’ box, of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, who both jumped up in celebration? They were far more animated than Carrick and could not contain themselves.

"Football is a contact sport!" 🗣️ Did Senne Lammens foul Zion Suzuki for Man United's equaliser? 🤔 https://t.co/KCb1lHqPHP

Did their behaviour betray not just their excitement in the moment but their relief at not having to sack Carrick during this forthcoming international break? If so, they need to think again. They need to make a sober and rational decision based on evidence. And the evidence shows that Carrick must go. Because this kind of football is unsustainable. This kind of football does not work. This kind of football is stupid.

United are 18th in the Premier League. They have won one game in 10 in the league. They have conceded 15 goals in their last five matches in the league and Champions League. When they play Liverpool away, their next game, on November 22, it will be the first time they have done so from inside the relegation zone since March 1937.

They appear shockingly disorganised. Tactics seem to be an after-thought, their motivation is lacking until desperation kicks in. United conceded two goals within four minutes at the start of the game. And then two more within eight minutes of the second half kicking off.

The bottom line is this: can they afford not to make a change? If they do not, United could be accused of copping out and gambling with their status. So, Berrada and Wilcox must ask: what is Carrick doing in the dressing room and on the training ground? What messages are he and his assistant Steve Holland sending out? Are the players even listening?

At the end the fans sang Carrick’s name after United became the first team in the Premier League to come back twice from being two goals down. That also summed up the fog of confusion at a club who so obviously lack direction – from the top down – and need to get a grip of themselves. Carrick talked about having to “tighten up” the defending. But everything needs to be stronger. More taut. More competitive.

Chaos can be entertaining. Chaos can be fun. As an advert for the Premier League this was outstanding. United fans will be thrilled with the Fergie-time comeback. But chaos is also unsustainable. No one knows what to expect from United.

In the cold light of day Villa manager Unai Emery will have to ask himself whether he, too, got it wrong. His substitutions did not work, bizarrely taking off too much experience, such as his outstanding captain John McGinn, and he handed United a late initiative when it looked like all hope was lost.

But analyse the goals that United conceded. Any rational response would suggest a change should be made. Take the first two. Villa scored with their first attack, moving the ball from a throw-in, with zero pressure on them, from left to right with McGinn finding Alysson. The winger’s low first-time shot went through the legs of goalkeeper Senne Lammens, who had an awful game. Michael Carrick has insisted he remains the right man to lead Manchester United and will not walk away despite the club being marooned in the relegation zone.

United came from 2-0 and 4-2 down to claim a last-gasp 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on another wild day at Old Trafford.It means United still only have one Premier League win to their name this season and are languishing in 18th position, a point adrift of safety, heading into the international break when the Old Trafford hierarchy must decide whether to keep faith with Carrick or appoint their third manager this year.

Carrick cut a spiky figure when asked about his future by Sky Sports and whether he would walk away.

“That’s not going to happen,” Carrick said, before asking “will there?” when it was put to him that there would “clearly” be conversations about his future.

“We haven’t won enough games, but I expect to move forward and keep working on the things we’ve been working on and showing a lot of good in the game today,” he said. “Tighten up on some things and start winning football matches.”

“I like what he brings to the team, I like what he brings to the group, I like what he brings to the whole environment and the culture that we’ve got.”

Asked if Dalot needed taking out of the team for his own good, Carrick: “Picking a team and who plays the next game, that’s a whole different decision, but it’s a whole different game that we’ve got to look forward to now.

Unai Emery stormed straight down the tunnel before the final whistle, furious at his team’s failure to see out the game.

With four Premier League games in progress the picture is ever-changing, but United are currently 19th in the Premier League table. The club, famously, were relegated in 1974 with the coup de grâce applied by Denis Law’s backheel when the Scot was playing in a City shirt. In this piece, James Ducker looks back on the previous occasions when one of the world’s biggest clubs has flirted with calamity.

When Villa dropped into the Championship, it did not change the fact they were the biggest club in the Midlands. No matter what Tom Brady does at Birmingham City, that’s not changing any time soon. They sought and achieved promotion by raiding Brentford.

Nobody was complaining about a sleeping giant taking Dean Smith, Ezri Konsa or Ollie Watkins and potentially stalling Brentford’s progression.

Nor was it suggested hiring Emery from Villarreal was an odd move given that the Spanish side had recently won the Europa League and reached the latter stages of the Champions League.

Michael Carrick says he has been given no assurances about his future beyond this afternoon’s crucial game against Aston Villa at Old Trafford.United are searching for only their second Premier League win of the season and first in 70 days after the club’s worst start to a campaign for 40 years piled the pressure on Carrick.They dropped into the relegation zone last night following Nottingham Forest’s victory over Manchester City and will be bottom by the end of the weekend if they lose to Villa and Crystal Palace and Sunderland both win.The Old Trafford hierarchy opted to give Carrick more time to try to turn their season around following a 3-0 hammering by Bournemouth and 4-1 drubbing in Como, since when United have been beaten 2-0 by Chelsea and recovered from two goals down to overcome Roma 3-2 in the Champions League on Tuesday night.Asked if he had been told outright he would still be in charge next week, Carrick said: “No - no. Just carry on as absolute normal.”Pressed on when he felt his future was uncertain, the head coach added: “No, no. Whatever happens and what’s going to happen is going to happen in terms of the game, we’ve got to prepare right.“I’m really looking forward to playing at home on the back of the other night. The supporters are hopefully looking forward to coming and energised and feeling good about what they might see and we’ve got to repay that.”Another defeat would leave the United board with a big decision to make around Carrick’s future at a time when they are under severe attack from the fanbase.United’s game against Roma was briefly interrupted when tennis balls were thrown on to the pitch in the first half of a game notable for more furious protests against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe.Three people were arrested by Greater Manchester Police for throwing items on to the pitch and are understood to have been hit with automatic three-year football banning orders as a consequence. More in-stadium demonstrations are expected today with regular match going fans encouraged not to buy alcohol or drinks inside Old Trafford and again release green and gold balloons before kick-off.Green and gold were the club’s original colours as Newton Heath and have become a symbol of protest against the ownership. Asked why there had been such a big drop-off from last season, Carrick added: “It’s just inconsistency, that’s within games,” he said.“It can be a number of things, it’s never just one thing: a bit of decision-making, a bit of concentration, things going against us in certain points, sometimes we haven’t helped ourselves. So there’s no excuses for it, it is what it is. The great thing is we can do something about it.”

#1047. Michael Carrick sacked LIVE: Man Utd part ways with manager and move to complete Pochettino deal

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The former United midfielder was let go today after the club’s worst start to a domestic season in 40 years

Michael Carrick has been sacked as Manchester United manager after overseeing the club’s worst start to the Premier League season in 40 years, with Mauricio Pochettino looking set to replace him.

A second Old Trafford comeback of the week, this time battling from two goals down twice to rescue a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday, was not enough to save Carrick’s job and the club announced on Thursday that it had parted ways with him after just 10 games of the season and with his side 18th during the international break.

United ended a nine-game winless run when they came from two goals down to beat Roma in the Champions League last week but they have not won in eight attempts in the Premier League and have just one top-flight win this campaign.

Carrick survived crisis talks with the United hierarchy after defeats to Como and Bournemouth last month and was given time to turn results around, but speculation over a change begun the day after Sunday’s chaotic draw and The Independent understands contact was initially made with United States boss Pochettino over succeeding Carrick on Monday.

The Old Trafford hierarchy, including Jason Wilcox, Omar Berrarda and Sir Jim Ratcliffe, met in Monaco to discuss Carrick’s future and the club are on the verge of hashing out a deal with Pochettino, who is reportedly ready to accept the position.

Follow latest updates from Old Trafford here:

Paul Scholes thinks Man United might be going in for Mauricio Pochettino a few years too late.

He said on The Good, The Bad & The Football: “I love Pochettino and we work with him at Soccer Aid, didn’t we, he’s a he’s a great man. I think he’s got the presence to manage a big football club like Manchester United.

“He’s got the respect to do it. He works with young players which obviously Manchester United want. My only slight concern is have that we come a little bit too late to the party.

“I think we’ve done that in the past. You look at Van Gaal, his best years were probably behind him. Mourinho again, I think his best years were probably behind him. Saying that, I’m not ruling out what he’s going to do with this Real Madrid team because this Real Madrid team look good.

“I just - when you really think about when we was talking about this two or three weeks ago after the Bournemouth game I don’t think any of us mentioned Pochettino.”

The Manchester United Supporters’ Trust (MUST) has branded Michael Carrick’s sacking “another depressing moment” and argued the club’s problems rest primarily with its ownership, in a now-familiar plea to end the ongoing feeling of crisis at Old Trafford.

United sacked Carrick just 10 games into the Premier League season with the club in the relegation zone and having won just once in this domestic campaign.

The club’s hierarchy met minority owner Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco on Wednesday to discuss Carrick’s future and a statement on Thursday said that it had “come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions”.

Today is only the sixth time in Premier League history two managers - Michael Carrick and Pierre Sage - have left their positions on the same day during a season.

The last time it happened actually wasn’t that long ago, with Wolves boss Gary O'Neil and Southampton manager Russell Martin both getting canned on 15 December 2024.

Pochettino is still contracted to US Soccer until the 2030 World Cup though an early departure from his deal feels increasingly likely. United have made contact with US Soccer over paying compensation to release Pochettino with rumoured figures reaching as high a $10m (£7.4m).

Should an agreement be made, Pochettino could, in theory, leave the US before the scheduled games against Haiti in order to spend time with Man United’s squad ahead of the crucial clash at Anfield.

In that case he could arrive at Carrington either the same day or a day after being formally announced as the new head coach. That would give him a maximum of nine days to prepare the team if his appointment is confirmed today (Thursday 12 November).

The more likelier option is that Pochettino leads the USMNT for their two fixtures with Haiti and reports to Carrington shortly afterwards.

In that case, he could be in post at Man United as early as Wednesday 18 November though given the time difference between the US and the UK, Pochettino would arrive late in the afternoon or early evening.

Even so, that would give him three full days, Thursday 19, Friday 20 and Saturday 21 to settle into his new environment and have time on the grass with the squad.

Thoughts have now turned to Michael Carrick’s replacement with former Tottenham, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain manager Mauricio Pochettino the odds on favourite to take over.

Pochettino is the current manager of the United States Men’s National Team (USMNT) but has reportedly reached a verbal agreement with Man United to sign of as their new head coach. Should his appointment be confirmed when will Pochettino officially begin his tenure?

Man United’s next match comes on Sunday 22 November when they travel to Anfield to take on Liverpool. It will arguably be the most difficult start possible for whoever takes over and it is a game United need to take something from or else they risk dropping further into the relegation zone.

The current international break would usually provide a new manager with time to train and see the squad in action but Pochettino, should he be given the job, is unlikely to have such a luxury.

That is because the United States have two Nations League matches to play on November 14 and 18 during this window and Pochettino is likely to oversee both fixtures.

Gary Neville has branded Manchester United ‘classless’ over how they handled the dismissal of Michael Carrick.

United finally pulled the trigger on Carrick’s sacking after days of leaving their manager in limbo, despite it becoming near-common knowledge that the club had been speaking to Mauricio Pochettino in an effort to acquire him as his replacement.

Speaking on the Overlap’s Stick to Football podcast, which was recorded prior to Thursday’s confirmation, he said: “We’re sat here today recording this programme knowing that Michael Carrick is going to be sacked tomorrow, knowing that they’re speaking to Mauricio Pochettino, knowing that they’ve spoken to (Julian) Nagelsmann, (Eddie) Howe – and they should be doing that by the way, I’m not saying they shouldn’t be doing that…

“But I think the fact they’re in Monaco now and they can’t sack him today knowing that it’s happening, to me it just feels a little bit clumsy, it feels a little bit classless.

“I think if you live in Monaco, you can’t leave a guy hanging for 24 or 48 hours just because you live in Monaco, that can’t happen.”

Manchester United are closing in on a deal to appoint Mauricio Pochettino before their next game against Liverpool following Michael Carrick’s sacking.

United must strike a deal with US Soccer, with a solution required over the United States’ next two international games in particular, while the club’s hierarchy is meeting at a Monaco summit to finalise a decision over the club’s manager.

Compensation, worth an initial $7m (£5.3m), will be a formality due to the clause in Pochettino’s existing contract, that runs until the 2030 World Cup.

But one major hurdle remains to ensure Pochettino can arrive in time for the trip to Anfield.

Rio Ferdinand has shown his support for former Manchester United team-mate Michael Carrick after his sacking.

“Forever legend!” he posted on X. “Showed dignity and class as always.”

He later criticised the club’s official statement confirming his exit, posting: “Man United statement like ChatGPT... I wanna hear a voice!”

Manchester United’s penchant for implosion during the first half of the season, often after a summer of intense financial backing, is quite evident from this stat.

The club’s last five permanent managers have all been sacked between 28 October and 5 January.

It’s almost as if recruitment and management are not aligned...

Crystal Palace have sacked manager Pierre Sage after the club slumped to bottom of the Premier League table for the first time since December 2017.

The Frenchman moved to Selhurst Park on a three-year contract this summer after an impressive year at Lens, where he led the club to a runner-up finish in Ligue 1, won the Coupe de France and Trophee des Champions titles for the first time, and qualified for the Champions League.

But he was unable to replicate that success across his 16 games in all competitions at Palace, who have conceded the most goals of any top-flight side this season and claimed just seven points out of a possible 30 during his tenure, and sit two points off safety going into the November international break.

#1044. Pierre Sage sacked by Crystal Palace

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Frenchman departs after a fourth consecutive Premier League defeat and with the Eagles bottom of the table

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Crystal Palace have sacked manager Pierre Sage after the club slumped to bottom of the Premier League table for the first time since December 2017.

The Frenchman moved to Selhurst Park on a three-year contract this summer after an impressive year at Lens, where he led the club to a runner-up finish in Ligue 1, won the Coupe de France and Trophee des Champions titles for the first time, and qualified for the Champions League.

But he was unable to replicate that success across his 16 games in all competitions at Palace, who have conceded the most goals of any top-flight side this season and claimed just seven points out of a possible 30 during his tenure, and sit two points off safety going into the November international break.

A club statement released on Thursday said: “Crystal Palace Football Club can confirm that Pierre Sage has left his role as Manager.

“The club would like to place on record its thanks to Pierre and his staff for their efforts during their time in South London, and wish them well for the future.

“An update on the process of appointing a new Manager will be provided in due course.”

Former Brentford and Tottenham manager Thomas Frank could be considered as Palace now attempt to rescue themselves from a relegation fight, while former Burnley, Everton and Nottingham Forest boss Sean Dyche is also out of work and would be available.

Three members of Sage’s coaching staff, Jamal Alioui, Damien Della Santa and Sandy Guichard, have also departed.

Sage leaves after a 3-1 defeat to Liverpool at Selhurst Park, which marked Palace’s fourth straight league loss and seventh in the top-flight this season. Palace also have one win, two draws and one defeat from four Europa League games and are through to the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup, where they play Sunderland next month.

The former Lyon boss had replaced perhaps the most successful Crystal Palace manager in modern history in Oliver Glasner, who won the FA Cup and Conference League with the Eagles before moving to Premier League rivals Nottingham Forest at the end of last season.

The former Sunderland goalkeeper admits he was dismissive of the idea of moving to the north-east of England

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where do you want to live? Cultured Amsterdam? The beautiful old city of Udine, near Venice? Or Sunderland?

We sincerely don't mean that as a slam on the north-east town, either.

After all, that's the decision young Danish goalkeeper Thomas Sorensen faced when deciding his next career move back in 1998 - and he picked the move to Wearside.

Sorensen told FourFourTwo: "I have my parents to thank for that.

"I was talking to a few clubs, like Ajax and Udinese, who had a long history of Danish players.

"Then this left-field offer came in from Sunderland. I hadn’t heard a lot about them and I sort of dismissed it.

"My mum and dad told me to go over and have a look. I was blown away.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I knew that this was the right thing for me. I would get an opportunity to play, I loved the feel of the northeast and their passion for football.

"It was probably one of the best decisions I ever made. "

Sorensen does admit that he had to adapt a little bit to Peter Reid's unique management style, however.

He said: "I had to get used to all the swearing!

"He was a great manager. One of the old school. He was probably the last manager I had who would allow the players to go out and have a few drinks.

"He cherished that camaraderie. He really encouraged the players to spend a lot of time together and that was probably part of our success.

"He said things as they were. He could be quite tough, but he was fair."
