#1014. Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action

Delap’s talents resurface in style, Gómez delights Brighton with more fireworks, and hair-pulling confusion at Everton

It would have been very easy for Oliver Glasner to lose patience with Liam Delap. The forward is still only 23, yet the days when he was rattling in 12 in a Premier League season for Ipswich have come to seem a very long time ago (and his six games for Manchester City even longer). A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. After games such as this it’s possible to imagine him as England’s long-term replacement for Harry Kane. Jonathan Wilson

Match report: Nottingham Forest 3-1 Manchester City

Amid the chaotic blur of proceedings at Old Trafford, there was one outstanding performance. Alysson had only one goal to his name in his Premier League career at Aston Villa, but he scored one and helped set up another two in the first 48 minutes against Manchester United. The 20-year-old winger, who has represented Brazil only at under-16 level, was signed from Grêmio for an initial £8.7m last January. His only goal in 18 previous appearances was against Nottingham Forest in September – it took less than a minute to open the scoring at United and less than four for his saved shot to rebound out to Nicolas Jackson for Villa’s second. United’s right-back, Diogo Dalot, was too slow to close Alysson down for his opener and did not have any complaints when his trip on the Brazilian conceded a penalty at the start of the second half. Dalot, often the face of United’s struggles, was booed off when substituted in the second half – Alysson was applauded off by the away end. Billy Munday

Match report: Manchester United 4-4 Aston Villa

Diego Gómez is the latest example of a slow-burning Brighton player given the chance and space to bed in before then flourishing. His current status is as an overnight sensation, though a taste for the spectacular and an eye for goal have been obvious since two goals against Leeds in November 2025. Gómez had signed from Inter Miami that January. The inside-right position from which he drilled his left-foot sidewinder to open the scoring against Brentford brings the best from his shooting prowess with both feet. His October halfway line strike against Crystal Palace came with his right foot. As with a number of Brighton’s purchases, Gómez can play in other positions, variously defensive midfielder, attacking midfielder, even on the wing. Within Fabian Hürzeler’s stringent tactical setup, he is asked to work hard for the ball. Such high pressing created the opportunity Charalampos Kostoulas should have done better with in the moments after the opening goal. John Brewin

There is nothing wrong with Arsenal’s habit of winning games by a single goal: Mikel Arteta’s side did it 15 times on their way to the title last season and the latest against Hull was their fourth this season. Yet despite being six points clear of Manchester City heading into the international break, Arteta will have some concerns about the lack of goals so far. With only 15 from their first 10 matches, Arsenal are on course to break Manchester United’s record of 67 for the fewest by a team being crowned champions in 1993 – the Premier League’s first season. They have also been struggling to score in the first half of games, having gone six matches in all competitions without doing so last month, and Arteta has called on his players to be more ruthless. “Sometimes we try to score the perfect goal against low blocks, but we need to be much more chaotic than that. If we open the scoring much earlier also, it changes the game,” he said. Ed Aarons

All hail Brian Brobbey. It is fascinating that a player sometimes derided for his supposed lack of technical quality while at Ajax has developed into one of the Premier League’s most potent and difficult-to-play centre-forwards in little more than a year in England. His new contract, announced last Wednesday, is richly deserved. There is, as Régis Le Bris acknowledged after the win over Chelsea in which he bullied the visitors, no one quite like him. “Against a team that wants to press like that it’s so important to have a target man,” said the Sunderland manager, and Brobbey was that and then some. Much has been made of how Chelsea miss João Pedro but the Mackems are a different team with their flying Dutchman. Andy Brassell

It was a tale of two benches at Elland Road. The big question hanging over Leeds is whether they have the support for Dominic Calvert-Lewin to make a concerted push for Europe this season; a question that went some way to being answered when the substitutes Harry Wilson and Noah Okafor combined for the latter to score the winner against Tottenham. In contrast, Roberto De Zerbi’s attacking options let him down in a game that felt there for the taking. Dominic Solanke struggled after replacing Mathys Tel, Omar Marmoush looked limited in the central striker role and their brightest performer was the 18-year-old Lucá Williams-Barnett, who, you would suspect, is now not far from a deserved start. Having won three straight games before their defeat in West Yorkshire, Spurs suddenly go into the international break with more questions than answers over their attacking credentials once again. Aaron Bower

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Andoni Iraola had one wish as he signed off for the international window with the 3-1 win at Crystal Palace – that he does not lose any players to injury before Liverpool are back in action against Manchester United at Anfield on Sunday week. The manager is scarred by the previous round of international fixtures: Dominik Szoboszlai, Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak all picked up problems. The trio were missed as Liverpool lost to Manchester City in the first game back. Szoboszlai’s injury was the most concerning: he was only able to return as a substitute in the defeat against Arsenal on 1 November and Iraola said after the win at Palace that the Hungary midfielder was not 100%, that a knee problem required management. “Let’s see if Dom can play with the national team or not,” Iraola said. “I know what I want! But I have to understand the national teams. Also I’m sure Dom will want to go. I’m not sure if it’s going to be fine.” David Hytner

Match report: Crystal Palace 1-3 Liverpool

Bournemouth are really getting to grips with the Thursday-Sunday grind in their first season in Europe. Marco Rose has been working hard to ensure his team are in the right shape to start Premier League games quickly after a Europa League assignment three days earlier. After Thursday’s trip to face Sparta Prague, Bournemouth were quick out of the traps at Ipswich on Sunday, taking the lead through Evanilson after five minutes. “Last week [against Leeds] I said we start slow and this week we start quite quick and score an early goal – I am a magician,” said the head coach, after their eighth consecutive win in all competitions. That equalled a club record set under Eddie Howe in League One. Evanilson is himself on a streak – he’s scored in five in a row in the league – and only Nicolas Jackson has scored as many in the top flight since the last international break. The Brazilian did not need Christian Walton’s helping hand with this goal. BM

Newcastle delivered one of their more convincing performances of the season at Fulham, but one area remains a headache for Matthias Jaissle. Efforts to replace Alexander Isak in attack have not been good enough. Nick Woltemade was loaned to Juventus after an inconsistent debut season in England and there was not much encouragement to take from how Yoane Wissa and William Osula played at Craven Cottage. Wissa, who has struggled since his £55m move from Brentford last summer, has four goals in 41 appearances and did not put himself about enough before being taken off after 61 minutes, while Osula did not manage a touch in Fulham’s area and lost possession before Rodrigo Muniz’s late equaliser for the hosts. Jaissle needs more from his forwards on and off the ball. Otherwise Newcastle are going to need to find different players to lead their attack. Jacob Steinberg

The laws on hair-pulling were changed for this season after the red cards that were issued to Michael Keane, Lisandro Martínez and Dan Ballard in 2025-26. They are undoubtedly an improvement but, as James Tarkowski’s pull on Caleb Yirenkyi’s hair demonstrated in Everton’s comeback against Coventry, grey areas remain. Frank Lampard and David Moyes agreed the Everton captain should not have been sent off as there was no excessive force involved. But was it “a clear action without excessive force” that should have resulted in a yellow card for unsporting behaviour and a penalty to Coventry? Or “negligible, accidental or inadvertent contact” that is not usually considered an offence? Moyes offered up one solution – scrap the law altogether. “I think it is still ridiculous that is even categorised in the rules of the game,” the Everton manager said. “I can’t understand why they don’t fix this completely because I don’t see it as a good rule at all.” Andy Hunter

#1011. Anderson, 44, joins Surrey for 2027 season

James Anderson was released by Lancashire after 2026 season, despite taking 50 wickets at an average of 17.68 as they finished second-bottom of Division Two; Surrey won three consecutive County Championship titles from 2022 to 2024; runners-up in 2025, they finished seventh last season

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

England great Sir James Anderson has joined Surrey ahead of the 2027 season in the Rothesay County Championship, continuing his career aged 44.

Anderson, England's all-time leading wicket taker, was released by boyhood club Lancashire in October after over 25 years with the county, a decision he said left him "sad" and "quite shocked" and made him question if there was something "fundamentally wrong with me as a person".

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Upon the announcement of his move to the Kia Oval, Anderson said: "It's an honour to join a club like Surrey and I can't wait to start a new chapter in my career.

"I still feel like I have a lot to offer, taking wickets, trying to help the team win games of cricket.

"I also think that I can bring a lot to the team off the field and help those young players who are looking to develop their skillset and go on and represent their country."

Anderson, who turns 45 in July of next year, will get the opportunity to add to his haul of 1,193 first-class wickets and perhaps more silverware to a glittering CV that includes four Ashes series victories and the 2010 T20 World Cup in the Caribbean.

The Burnley-born bowler picked up 50 wickets at an average of 17.68 in County Championship Division Two for Lancashire in 2026.

County cricket ins and outs - all the signings, departures and overseas arrivals ahead of the 2027 season

Cricket: James Anderson says he is 'excited' after signing for Surrey

'Sandpapergate': Australia captain Pat Cummins to address Usman Khawaja claims on Friday

Mitchell Marsh bats away 'Sandpapergate' questions

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

His exit from Old Trafford came as the hierarchy, including new director of cricket Paul Farbrace, plot to build an attack for the future after a poor few seasons in red-ball cricket.

Anderson captained Lancashire last term as the county finished second bottom of the second tier, ahead of only Gloucestershire.

Surrey have won the County Championship on 22 occasions, including three in a row from 2022 to 2024. They were runners-up in 2025 but had a disappointing 2026 campaign in which they finished seventh.

Surrey's director of men's cricket, Alec Stewart, said: "We're delighted to bring someone of the calibre of Sir James Anderson to Surrey.

"Jimmy brings quality with the ball. His 50 championship wickets last season prove that he is still one of the best bowlers in the country.

"Jimmy also brings a wealth of experience to the group that all our bowlers will learn from. Much of our squad have international aspirations, and they will learn a great deal from training, playing and being in the same dressing room with Jimmy."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Former Australia head coach Darren Lehmann, who is now in charge of Northamptonshipe, posted on X that his county were one of those to miss out on Anderson's signing.

Anderson - who is poised to play in the Italia T10 for Napoli Knights later this month - was forced into international retirement by England in 2024.

He took four wickets in his final Test, against West Indies at Lord's, to end with 704 wickets across 188 games in the longest format, at an average of 26.45.

He is the most prolific pace bowler in Test history, with only Sri Lankan off-spinner Muttiah Muralitharan (800) and Australian leg-spinner Shane Warne (708) taking more wickets.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

May 2002 - Anderson makes first-class debut for Lancashire; takes his maiden first-class wicket in May, dismissing Ian Ward.

December 15, 2002 - Anderson makes ODI debut for England against Australia in Melbourne, aged 20.

February-March 2003 - Anderson selected in England's squad for 2003 Cricket World Cup, producing match-winning spell against Pakistan. England lose to eventual champions Australia.

May 2003 - Anderson becomes youngest player to take a hat-trick in Lancashire history - the first at Old Trafford for eight years.

May 22, 2003 - Anderson makes Test match debut for England against Zimbabwe at Lord's, still aged 20. Takes five wickets in an innings on debut.

August 2003 - Anderson unanimously voted as England's Young Cricketer of the Year.

September 2003 - Anderson handed central contract with the ECB.

July 2005 - After period out of the England squad, Anderson is recalled for final Test of Ashes series, but fails to make team.

September-December 2006 - After a back stress fracture and six months out, Anderson returns to England side for Ashes series in 5-0 whitewash defeat in late 2006.

January 2007 - Anderson plays in his first T20 International, playing for England against Australia in Sydney.

2009 - Anderson is named one of five Wisden Cricketers of the Year following a standout Test series against in 2009 Ashes victory.

September 2011 - Anderson helps Lancashire win the County Championship title.

July 2014 - Batting at No 11, Anderson makes 81 against India, his highest Test total

March 2015 - Anderson plays his final ODI match for England against Afghanistan in Sydney.

April 2015 - Against West Indies, Anderson becomes England's record Test wicket-taker with his 384th dismissal.

July 25, 2016 - Anderson becomes first fast bowler to take 50 wickets against all other seven major Test-playing nations, Australia, India, New Zealand, Pakistan, South Africa, Sri Lanka and West Indies.

December 26, 2019 - Anderson becomes ninth cricketer to play in 150 Test matches.

January 5, 2020 - Anderson takes 28th five-wicket haul in Test cricket, overtaking Ian Botham's England record.

March 9, 2024 - Anderson becomes only third player in history to reach 700 career Test wickets

July 2024 - Anderson announces international retirement having played his 188th and final Test match for England against the West Indies at Lord's.

April 2025 - Knighthood | Appointed a Knight Bachelor in recognition of his services to cricket.

2025-2026 - Lancashire Captaincy & Contract. Returned briefly to T20 cricket, signed a one-year extension, and was named Lancashire red-ball captain for the 2026 County Championship season.

October 2026 - Anderson leaves Lancashire after contract not renewed

November 2026 - Joins Surrey ahead of 2027 County Championship season

#1010. You are Scotland boss Pocognoli - what would you do?

Nations League: Scotland v North Macedonia

Sebastien Pocognoli's first camp in charge of Scotland ended in gloomy fashion last month as Slovenia deservedly won 2-1 at Hampden.

The Belgian head coach has the chance to bounce back when his side face North Macedonia in Glasgow's southside on Friday, live on the BBC.

Scott McTominay, Kieran Tierney and Che Adams are all back in the national team squad for the closing Nations League double-header, which ends with a trip to Switzerland on Monday.

Put yourself in Pocognoli's shoes and pick your XI with our team selector below, while we have picked out some of the key selection dilemmas.

McTominay is sure to make his first appearance under Pocognoli, but where will the Belgian deploy the Napoli star?

The 29-year-old has been sitting slightly deeper in midfield for his club this season but has still managed five goals in 11 outings.

Pocognoli used a 3-4-2-1 or 3-4-1-2 formation across his first four games and McTominay could well be used with John McGinn behind a central striker, given the duo's impressive strike rate at international level.

Billy Gilmour and Lewis Ferguson were the starting central midfielders in all of Pocognoli previous matches, so is that an established long-term pairing or will Ryan Christie finally get the chance to show what he can do in the area where he has excelled with Bournemouth in recent years?

Of course, McTominay and McGinn are options in the middle of the pitch too.

The width is almost certainly going to come from wing-backs despite an unconvincing beginning to Pocognoli's preferred method.

Skipper Andy Robertson is a dead cert to start on the left as he closes in on the nation's caps record currently held by Sir Kenny Dalglish.

Ben Gannon-Doak started the last two games on the right but the little winger is not a natural fit in the position.

However, he was a dangerous attacking outlet in the 2-0 win away to North Macedonia and may be favourite to keep the jersey for an evening when Scotland are expected to have the lion's share of possession.

For the sterner test away to Switzerland, Aaron Hickey appears the obvious alternative.

Dalkeith to LA pays off for Porteous with Scotland recall

Pocognoli to lean on Scotland's 'captain group of five'

Oli McBurnie started the first four games of the Pocognoli era after ending his long exile from the squad and earned praise for his industry.

But here's the rub. The Hull City striker is still without a goal in 20 caps.

McBurnie is off the mark in the Premier League though, with two goals in his past three outings.

If Scotland revert to two up top at home to opponents that have not scored in eight matches, his place looks assured.

If it's down to one, then the manager might want a look at Adams or go with Kieron Bowie, who was on target with a cracking early strike against North Macedonia in October.

Like Robbie Ure at Sevilla, Bowie has lost his starting place at Sassuolo over the past three league matches, which could be a factor.

Jack Grealish's Everton travails could signal a death knell to the 'Gazza generation'

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Deep down, Jack Grealish will know that his fate extends beyond Everton's season.

English football’s first £100m player has won multiple Premier League titles and a Champions League yet still faces a fight to stave off the death knell to an increasingly lost generation as much as his own elite-level career.

Grealish again finds himself out in the cold after a ‘breach of club discipline’ in the run-up to Everton’s Carabao Cup win over Newcastle and was subsequently deemed unfit for the league rematch at St James’ Park on Monday night. On both occasions, David Moyes’s side were hardly poorer without the winger’s presence.

The Toffees are yet to decide on a definitive course of action over Grealish’s reported unauthorised absence from training, but patience is now in increasingly short supply from the club and its supporters alike. At a time when Moyes is dealing with crippling squad dearth - just 18 senior players were left after a disastrous summer window - the England international's latest misdemeanour threw him another needless curveball.

There was always a risk that Grealish's propensity to hit the headlines for the wrong reasons would again rear its head on Merseyside, where he claimed that feeling ‘loved’ in his initial loan spell was a driving factor in embarking on a second. Such was a fondness for his current surroundings that he undertook the bulk of his rehabilitation from a season-ending foot injury sustained in January at their Finch Farm training ground instead of returning to parent club Manchester City.

But even then, indiscretion was still lurking round the corner. When Everton slipped to a late April defeat at relegation candidates West Ham, Grealish was being snapped slumped against the arm of a chair in a Manchester rooftop bar surrounded by bottles and glasses. Now 31, he is in danger of completing an unholy trinity that was once touted for greatness as successors to Paul Gascoigne’s throne but allowed their careers to crash and burn.

Just 16 months separate the respective birth dates of the Birmingham-born talent, Dele Alli and Raheem Sterling. All three were alive when English football’s flawed genius enjoyed one last hurrah at Euro 96 but none will have any memories of it. That has still done little to stop their affection for ‘Gazzamania’ running deep.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Upon his return to Everton this summer, Grealish revealed he was partly inspired to take the No.18 shirt worn by Gascoigne during a forgettable and fleeting spell in the blue half of Merseyside while Sterling also cited the man that personified the 1990 World Cup as his all-time favourite Three Lions player. Even Dele, who himself previously sought redemption at Everton, made an embarrassing attempt at recreating the infamous ‘dentist’s chair’ celebration during a training session at Euro 2016.

They also appeared destined to follow in his footsteps by earning moves to high-profile leagues overseas with Real Madrid heavily touted as a future destination for each player. Beyond personal homages, Gascoigne has become intertwined with the trio as a quickfire buzzword for their respective rises to prominence. Individual billings as the ‘new Gazza’ also proved to be a self-fulfilling prophecy for a penchant for self-destruction mirroring the downfall of the former Rangers and Lazio playmaker. Dele is now 14 months into unofficial retirement and resorting to calling up former teammates live on Twitch streams in a desperate ploy to stay in the public consciousness. An awkward attempted catch-up with Harry Kane, just weeks before his old Tottenham sparring partner claimed the Ballon d’Or, lasted barely 60 seconds.

The depth of Dele's continental ambitions was short-lived spells with Besiktas and Como, making a solitary appearance for the latter before being released barely midway through an 18-month contract. Free agent Sterling fared far worse with a three-month spell at Feyenoord which was terminated last season. Grealish's former City teammate and fellow Euro 2020 standout faces the real prospect of ending this month behind bars as well as without a club after pleading guilty to dangerous driving while inhaling nitrous oxide and crashing his Lamborghini on the A327 in May.

Without sufficient intervention on his own part, Grealish may soon follow his former contemporaries in falling by the footballing wayside. More than most, he has been the poster boy for Gascoigne's heirs, as the man himself confirmed to FourFourTwo last year by singling out the former Aston Villa graduate as his closest embodiment in the current crop of players. His exploits in City’s 2023 treble-winning campaign hinted that England’s first Ballon d’Or winner since Michael Owen was closer than Kane’s recent triumph but never came to pass. What happens next will be era-defining.

Grealish is still capable of technical excellency, as demonstrated in a truncated first loan spell with Everton, if he can stave off personal indiscipline issues. He would not be the first homegrown talent to do so. Ross Barkley, another ex-teammate born in the mid-90s, was also festooned with the Gascoigne moniker yet managed to overcome his own off-field issues to earn a second chance at Villa. Persistent injuries prevented the playmaker from scaling even a fraction of the heights he was originally tipped to reach but used stints at Nice and Luton Town to rebuild his reputation and earn a bit-part role with Unai Emery’s side.

By personal admission, Grealish has been his own worst enemy when it comes to a sense of timing off the pitch which is at odds with an often impeccable nature on it. Unless he can conquer those social demons which ultimately brought down his idol as well as those in the same talent pool, the epitaph of the 'Gazza generation' will be one of frustratingly unfulfilled potential.

#1007. No excuses as Pocognoli seeks first Hampden victory

Sebastien Pocognoli is preparing for his fifth game in charge of Scotland

For Sebastien Pocognoli, Friday against North Macedonia is a third opportunity to replace the Hampden Bore with something akin to a Hampden Roar.

Two home games so far under the new head coach and two defeats; five goals conceded, one scored.

The loss to a superior Switzerland was written off because of an early red card for Jack Hendry. The loss to Slovenia had no such mitigation.

Scotland were creatively bereft, physically weak and tactically confused. Captain Andy Robertson said that his team had been out-played and out-fought.

For his own credibility, Pocognoli needs a big night. "Criticism is part of the business as a coach," he says. "It's just about rebounding." This is a huge chance to rebound.

Scotland beat North Macedonia 2-0 in Skopje in his third game in charge. They were without Scott McTominay, Kieran Tierney and Che Adams back then, but they're all in harness now. No excuses, in other words.

Pocognoli insists he learned a few things from that Slovenia game, saying: "We were not intense. We were not aggressive - and this is the one non-negotiable topic with me. We didn't deserve more in that game."

Nations League: Scotland v North Macedonia

Theoretically, Scotland are in better shape now than they were in the last four-game camp.

McTominay is back from his startling heart issues and is scoring again for Napoli. Tierney is one of only a few bright sparks at Celtic. Adams has scored two goals in five games in Italy since he missed the last international window.

There is other encouraging news. Scott Bain's shot-stopping form has to make him a major contender to usurp Angus Gunn in goal. San Jose Earthquakes have conceded eight goals in their last three games. Gunn was badly at fault for one and wasn't too clever for another. Bain has been making the kind of saves that look beyond Gunn.

Luke Graham continues to thrive at centre-back for Stoke City in the English Championship and must be a big option to start. Aaron Hickey has played more football since Slovenia than he did before it.

The same can be said of Ben Gannon-Doak. Before the last camp he had played six times for Bournemouth with an average of 18 minutes per game. Since then, he's played seven with an average of 53 minutes.

He was the man-of-the-match in a 3-0 win against AC Milan. Gannon-Doak must be in a much better place now, physically and mentally.

His club-mate, Ryan Christie, is in a very similar boat. He was more of a substitute than a starter for Bournemouth ahead of the last international break. Lately, he's been one of their go-to guys.

Christie has won eight games in a row with his club and he started in six of those. His confidence must be soaring.

You are Scotland boss Pocognoli - what would you do?

Dalkeith to LA pays off for Porteous with Scotland recall

Turkey-based Bates replaces Binks in Scotland squad

Kieron Bowie is having a difficult time at Sassuolo and Robbie Ure is in-and-out of the Sevilla team, but he scored twice for them last month. Oli McBurnie's painful wait for a Scotland goal carries on, but he has two in his last three for Hull in the Premier League.

Pocognoli says he has no fixed system, no slavish adherence to his favoured back three. It does sound like he's sticking with it for North Macedonia, though.

"I try to find the best shape to make the players shine on the pitch," he says. "After that, it's up to them to show it. But I always try to adapt to my team. I think the shape that we play is the best shape to fit the best quality of the team.

"At Union Saint-Gilloise, when we became champions, we played three at the back because that was the system of the club.

"Sometimes I felt like, if we try a back four, maybe we can have more power in the game, but I didn't do it because the club was building. In Monaco when I make the analysis of the squad, the best shape was a back three, but sometimes we played with a back four.

"It depends on the players' abilities. I believe for this team, right now, it's one of the best shapes. It's a brave style of play that demands a lot of energy. But it's a process. You need to analyse what is good for the future."

Scott McTominay reveals he underwent heart procedure days before World Cup game

Pocognoli feels his team lacked some freshness in the defeat by Slovenia and appears to have some regrets about that, adding: "Maybe we should have rotated a little bit more in the game. That's maybe something that we can reflect on."

What's the big message of the camp so far?

"Continuity and improvement," is the reply. "The main message to the players is try to impress me, try to show that you want to produce something special next season [for the Euros campaign]."

McTominay's presence can only add to Scotland's potential goal threat.

On Tuesday, the Napoli midfielder spoke about his heart issues at the World Cup and his cardiac ablation operation in September.

The fact that he has scored five goals in his past six games for Napoli is testament to not just his ability but his mental and physical strength and his huge desire to kick-on. Pocognoli is thrilled to have him.

"He brings experience," he says. "He's a leader. The age average is quite low in the squad, so it's a massive impact for us to have him back - a player who can pass the message to the young generation and show them direction."

On Friday, that direction needs to be forward with accuracy, speed, aggression and goals.

Whatever formation is deployed against North Macedonia - four defeats out of four with no goals scored and 10 conceded - it needs to deliver an emphatic home win at the third time of asking.

#1006. Manchester City’s weaknesses under Enzo Maresca are being exposed

After three straight defeats, City’s manager says he will use the international break to reassess. Their problems may go beyond tactics

Enzo Maresca seemed, if not quite baffled by his side’s Saturday defeat to Nottingham Forest, then at least a little put out. After seven straight wins from the start of the season, that’s now three straight defeats, a pattern so unusual that it’s been recorded only once before in top-flight English history, by Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05. The three defeats were all different, Maresca said, although in all of them City had had more possession and more chances.

In the 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa two weeks ago, City had 63% of the ball and had 15 chances to Villa’s eight. In the 1-0 home defeat to Brighton last weekend, they had 62% possession and 21 chances to seven. At the City Ground, it was 79% possession and 12 chances to 11. So Maresca is right in one way: City could look at basic statistics and say they had been unfortunate – although Forest could equally point to the fact that they went into that game third top of the expected goals table but second-bottom of the actual table.

But there is another statistic that should concern Maresca: City have not kept a clean sheet since their victory at Anfield after the last international break, nine games ago. And the game before that, they let in three against Sunderland. In those last eight games, City have conceded 17 goals. It’s true that three of those can at least in part be blamed on errors by Gianluigi Donnarumma, but there are also structural issues. City have a vulnerability in transition that Forest ruthlessly exploited, a weakness not unfamiliar to Maresca’s teams. One of the criticisms he received at both Leicester and Chelsea was that his sides were often extremely cautious in possession, but that makes sense given how high a line he likes to play.

That’s also why duels are so crucial to his teams; losing possession immediately exposes a high back four. Maresca was visibly disappointed at the way City were outfought in the first half against Forest. Lose the ball and the opposition has a run at a back four with space behind it. That is always going to be a problem but especially so when the opposing center-forward is a Liam Delap who has just remembered how to play and is determined to make somebody pay for a year and a bit of disappointing form.

Yet the midfield Maresca picked was clearly vulnerable to being outmuscled. He clearly rates Enzo Fernández extremely highly, to the point that City paid £125m ($167.7m) to sign him from Chelsea. But Fernández, for all his gifts as a footballer, is not especially physical by the standards of the Premier League. When he and Cole Palmer played together, there was often a sense that it made Chelsea a little lightweight. Maresca, though, was so determined to field the Argentinian that he would come up with complex tactical solutions, such as using Malo Gusto as a weird right-back-cum-No-10 hybrid.

City are running into similar problems. Rayan Cherki is an enormously gifted attacking midfielder, but not one who can be relied upon defensively, either in terms of his positioning or his willingness to make tracking runs, something Pep Guardiola acknowledged last season. He can be physically outmatched. That is not necessarily a huge problem with two mobile runners behind him: ideally an Elliot Anderson-style shuttler and a more defensive holding and/or ball-winning presence like Rodri. But Rodri has gone and Fernández leaves Anderson with a huge amount of the physical work to do. If Anderson happens not to be on the spot – if, say, a defender loses the ball in a dangerous area, or a break bypasses him – City are very quickly exposed.

Maresca said he will use this international break to reassess, that this was a rare example where it was better for a team not to have another game straight away to try to put a defeat behind them. Perhaps there is a tactical solution to be found. Perhaps even one that isn’t just: don’t play Fernández and Cherki together. But he must also be aware that by the time the Premier League returns, City could be out of the title race, or effectively even out of the Premier League itself.

It was during the last international break that the independent panel announced City had been found guilty of all but one of the charges brought against them by the Premier League. There is a school of thought that the sanctions could be announced during this international break. It’s all but impossible, of course, to know precisely how it’s affecting players to play under the cloud of a potential huge points deduction, but if initial defiance has faded into a sullen acceptance, that may also lead to battles being lost, to a lack of intensity and desire.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

The issue is tactical, but it may not only be tactical.

#1001. Football Daily | Manchester United, Aston Villa and the unseriousness of a 4-4 draw

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

Precisely 13,266 games have been played since the inception of the Premier League, and 19 of those matches have finished 4-4 (0.1%), a rarity in a division dominated by the mighty 1-0 (17.6%). It was about time we got one, though. The months of August and September, when teams are still fighting to define their top-flight seasons and fitness and motivation tend to be at their peak, have never seen a single 4-4 draw. As motivation decreases the chances of stupid scorelines increase, and that’s where the 4-4 creeps in. There’s a certain on-the-beachness inherent in the score, and it is no coincidence that it has occurred more in the second half of April, as thoughts drift to the close season and the ineffable pointlessness of a lot of late-campaign football becomes unavoidable, than in the entirety of any other month.

Though scoring four goals in a single game is quite encouraging, conceding four in the same one is suggestive of poor planning. Of the 22 clubs to have been involved in a Premier League 4-4, half are no longer in the Premier League at all. Only Manchester City in 2023-24 have played out a 4-4 draw and won the league in the same season, while six teams have recorded the scoreline and promptly gone down. It is an inherently unserious score, which duly attracts unserious teams. Manchester United, being as they were a very serious team for a long while after its creation, had won the Premier League 11 times before they were involved in one. When they drew 4-4 with Everton in late April (obviously) 2012 it was their first 4-4 draw since 1974. Sunday’s against Aston Villa was their second in a year.

The effect is obviously quite discombobulating. Fans at Old Trafford on Sunday, as United fell two goals down, recovered, fell two goals down again and recovered again, didn’t know whether to laugh, cry, boo, cheer, leave early or stay late and most chose a combination. “I thought we were by far the better team,” cooed Michael Carrick, the obviously nice guy currently being forced to find awkward ways of looking on the bright side in generally miserable post-match interviews. “They started, scored, then we played some very, very good football. We were the better team for large parts of the game. We’re making it difficult for ourselves with the goals we’re giving away.”

He may be on to something there. United have now conceded first in 80% of their home games this season, a figure only Crystal Palace, also the only team with fewer points than them, can match, and his team’s chances of success would probably improve if they stopped doing it. And then there’s Villa, new masters of this silly scoreline, the club who in 1995 were involved in the Premier League’s first ever 4-4 draw and have now also played in the most recent, in the process moving joint top of the all-time 4-4 charts. Inevitably the teams most likely to have secured many of these have tended to be both rubbish enough to go around drawing 4-4 and also not quite rubbish enough to also get relegated, bad enough to concede loads of goals yet also good enough to score quite a few. This does feel like prime Everton territory but it is Tottenham – who lead the all-time Premier League goal concession rankings – and Villa – still the only team to draw 4-4 twice in the same season, back in 2007-08 – who have more than anyone else. Their running tally of 4-4 draws? Why, 4-4, obviously.

De Graafschap ⁠had announced ​that supporters had been barred from attending the match in Arnhem after groups failed to ⁠reach an agreement with authorities over a ticket allocation cut and other security measures. “We want to let the initial emotion subside and get a full picture of everything before we come with a further substantive response,” sighed De Graafschap.

Manchester United are set to appoint Mauricio Pochettino as their new boss

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United are finalising a deal to appoint Mauricio Pochettino as their new manager.

The Red Devils have endured a poor start to the season, finding themselves 18th in the Premier League with just three wins in all competitions, after climbing to third last term.

With Michael Carrick now hanging by a thread, the club have made the decision to replace the former midfielder – and United States men's national team coach Pochettino is now “the chosen candidate”.

After a successful interim spell in the second half of last season, Manchester United hired Michael Carrick on a two-year deal.

Following the poor start to the season, however, the club have decided to part with the former midfielder, with David Ornstein delivering an exclusive on the situation at Carrington.

The prolific journalist revealed in The Athletic that United are finalising a deal for the Argentine coach, terms ongoing with with his camp.

Yesterday, it emerged that Pochettino would “jump at the chance” to depart the USMNT for Old Trafford, with United CEO Omar Berrada favouring the move.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Ornstein has added that United are “yet to contact US, but straightforward should plan proceed”.

Pochettino has been in charge of the United States side since 2024, when he and Emma Hayes left the men's and women's Chelsea teams, respectively, to head Stateside.

The 54-year-old has been linked with the United job for as long as a decade, too, with his good work at Tottenham Hotspur seeing him in the running the Old Trafford hot seat a number of times over the years.

#997. Football Daily | ‘Where the hell is Roy Keane!’ Fifty shades of great football debate

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

Forget about Michael Carrick. Don’t dwell on Women’s Bigger Cup. Fret not about Pierre Sage. No, the big football story of the day is Big Website’s Ultimate 1-50, a rundown of the male footballers best associated with each squad number. It’s lighthearted reading designed to entertain, maybe even inform, and perhaps spark a few memories and a touch of debate. Or, if you prefer, a rage-bait waste of time that shames the internet. Where the hell is Roy Keane! How dare you leave out Bobby Moore! And Pelé? A list without Pelé? I don’t want to live in a world where there are lists without Pelé. Such is the world these days, though surely a certain amount of respect is due to an exercise that shuns Lionel Messi and Zinedine Zidane but can welcome in Salvatore Sirigu and Mateusz Klich. And true, it might be a challenging read for those (and, let’s be clear, we’re absolutely definitely not referring to ourselves here, no sirree) old enough to have been brought up in an era of 1; 2, 5, 6, 3; 7, 4, 8, 11; 9 (big man), 10 (little man). The days of two substitutes who wore Nos 12 and 14. The days of a quarter of wine gums in your pocket and misty rain drifting across the floodlights and … oh my god Asamoah Gyan is wearing No 3 and playing up front. This is not a drill. Repeat this is not a drill. Burn it all down, the game’s gone. There is something about it all that does invoke strangely strong reactions, but every day is a school day. So, yes, there remains a hallowed aura around 1-11 but even some of the game’s greats – we’re looking at you Gerd Müller and Johan Cruyff – are best associated with numbers outside of the traditional undectet. And, as Jonathan Wilson brilliantly illustrates here, there’s a risk of being a bit Eurocentric when it comes to numbering – Argentina’s tactical evolution, for example, meant their traditional back four lines up 4, 2, 6, 3, with the No 5 in central midfield. Brazil too has No 5 as the defensive midfielder, with the standard back four as 4, 2, 3, 6. And don’t get us started on Hungary at Wembley in 1953 – Nandor Hidegkuti, you rascal! So do yourself a favour and dig into today’s offering. You might learn something. Or you might just get really, really cross about Curtis Jones. Either way, it’s win-win.

The FSA Awards are fast approaching folks and, though Football Daily has been cruelly overlooked yet again, Big Website has been nominated for a gong as well as Football Weekly, Women’s Football Weekly and Suzanne Wrack. If you want to show your support by casting a vote, you can here.

Join Billy Munday for piping hot MBM coverage of Inter 1-3 Manchester City in the Women’s Bigger Cup from 8pm GMT.

“If I look back on my own personal experience as a professional player, when I won the [Rumbelows] Cup I played with a broken ankle for 90 minutes, so that gives you the answer if I want to win or not. Let’s be honest, selling off the World Cup behind the back of the Fifa Council, the whole Fifa family, it’s a full betrayal. Morally and ethically it is unacceptable. And if [GIanni Infantino] had the balls, he would go out in front of 200 ⁠cameras, put his hands up and say ’yes, I made a mistake, I resign’” – Ramon Vega gets the battle-fever on as he talks about the combative qualities he hopes can transform him from underdog to top dog when he stands in the Fifa presidential election.

double quotation markAppreciate it’s all highly subjective but quite how you can give the all-time No 17 shirt to Kevin De Bruyne without so much as a mention of the legendary Pelly Ruddock Mpanzu is beyond me. What other player has gone from non-league to Premier League with the same club? OK, it’s a bit niche but a far more worthy winner in my completely unbiased (honest guv) opinion” – Kev Goddard.

double quotation markAll this talk of 4-4 draws (yesterday’s Football Daily) is very intoxicating for Chesterfield fans of a certain vintage. First up, the 1992 draw at Anfield where we threw away a 4-1 lead after a Liverpool comeback inspired by Istvan Kozma (no, really). Dave Lancaster scored two that night and observed that he had thought beforehand there might be eight goals in it, but not that we’d score four of them. And then in 2004 at Saltergate against Grimsby, where we threw away a 3-2 lead to go 4-3 down, before equalising with a last-minute penalty thanks to David Reeves. The attendance that day was 4,444. Makes you think …” – David Ede.

double quotation markTo stop managers continually going outside their technical areas, why not erect a ‘banners and poles’ surround, the sort of thing you see on pavements outside pubs and cafes? If the idea sounds a bit too simple, just mention the opportunity of more advertising space” – Peter Storch.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … David Ede. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

#996. 'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

If someone would've said to me I'd be doing this as a job when I was 12, I wouldn't have believed them.

My name's Jacob. I'm a content creator, and I work with Bolton Wanderers.

My role here at Bolton is coming up with new ideas for social media, to try new concepts, filming stuff, and then posting them onto Bolton's pages and trying to help people follow the club. In my opinion, I think it's one of the funnest jobs in football, and it's brilliant.

Right. Welcome to Bolton, Larra. I hope I said that right. I'm going to teach you some Bolton twang to help you settle in.

My passion for football when I was growing up started at a very young age. My dad used to take me to the football matches, and I got my very first season ticket when I was five years old in the 2010/11 season, when Bolton was in the Premiership. Being something I loved as a kid, to turn it into my job is amazing.

I work here at least two days a week, obviously filming content, producing content,and then on match day, I'll be filming mostly with fans, and I love it.

As a town? Well, for us, it's lovely. Yeah.

Mondays, meetings. We have the marketing meeting, so that gives you an idea of what the week holds, what I'm going to do on a match day with the fans. And then in the week, I either film in with players, retail, commercial,whatever department needs help producing videos.

Some of the skills I use, I think one of them's got to be communication. You've got to be able to talk to people, talk to fans, and if you're watching this and you're a bit shy, or you think you can't communicate with people as well, I was like that inhigh school, so you learn it as you get older. But working in football, you've got to be adaptable because one minute you're doing a new signing, next minute you're working with the players, next minute it's a match day, next minute the season's over.

I'd say another one is being creative. That's probably the most important one because without being creative, you won't be able to put a video together.

So when I was 16 in high school, that's where my journey started. I did videos, which got me a number of followers. I always struggled in the classroom side in high school, but creating content and creating ideas and being creative, I was always really, really good at in high school, whether that would be doing something drama-related or English, writing, creating stories. I always knew I had a passion for creative pieces of work and being able to now do it as a job, it suits me down to the ground.

I didn't go to college. I didn't go to uni. I left high school with no GCSEs, but I've always had a real passion for football, so that's how I got in contact with Bolton Wanderers. I started doing some videos here at Bolton with the fans and that, and then it turned into going to the training ground and filming with the players, working with the commercial team, retail team, all the different departmentsaround the football club to eventually getting a paid role in football.

I think don't wait for an opportunity to come to you. Get out there and try. If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role there. But if it doesn't, then you've also created a portfolio working with different people, different businesses, different companies, and it's really good for your CV and for future opportunities with different companies.

The highlight of my career so far, probably looking back, being resilient enough to create my own career path in doing something I love.

When you score this season, you might be chuffed.

If you're passionate about football, you're a bit creative, and you're good in front of the camera, content creation infootball might be a job for you.

To find out what other careers you can have in football, explore the BBC Bitesize Follow Your Passion collection.

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, coming up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posting them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Even as the children of German emigrants, Mark Schwarzer found life in Germany in the mid-1990s difficult.

A 21-year-old Schwarzer moved halfway across the world to join Dynamo Dresden from the Sydney-based Marconi Stallions in 1994, but played just twice before making the move west to Kaiserslautern the following season.

That gave Schwarzer a glimpse of life in both sides of what was then still a newly-reunified country - and he admits it was an eye-opening experience for a young man.

Schwarzer told FourFourTwo: "I loved parts of it, I hated others.

"It was 1994, only four years after unification between East and West Germany. Dresden was a beautiful city but very run down, with a huge period of rebuilding going on.

"There was still a real divide between East and West, and it could be difficult to fit in.

"I was a foreigner – I was German, but I wasn’t, because I was born in Australia. I was kind of in no man’s land.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I spoke a little German, but the local dialect was really difficult to understand.

"Australians weren’t regarded that highly as footballers either. We had the odd good player, but we weren’t really respected.

"I only played two games that season, but in hindsight the experiences I gained were invaluable.

"Kaiserslautern was similar and there was still a lack of acceptance because of where I came from.

"I played four games, did well in two, but my last was definitely my worst performance.

"Then Otto Rehhagel came in. He wasn’t a fan of young players and didn’t rate me. After two-and-a-half years in Germany, I knew I needed to find a club where the manager wanted me.

"I’d always wanted to play in England, and my wife could work there more easily, so when Bradford came along in November 1996, it was a no-brainer."

Steven Chicken has been working as a football writer since 2009, taking in stints with Football365 and the Huddersfield Examiner. Steven still covers Huddersfield Town home and away for his own publication, WeAreTerriers.com. Steven is a two-time nominee for Regional Journalist of the Year at the prestigious British Sports Journalism Awards, making the shortlist in 2020 and 2023.

#994. How to become a football referee

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your plan and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees new referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared."

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful."

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

Sources: National Careers Service, GOV.UK, FA, IFA, SFA, and FAW.

#993. Racing Bulls confirm 2027 line-up

After weeks of speculation, Liam Lawson's future at Racing Bulls is secure for another season; Lawson to again partner British youngster Arvid Lindblad at Red Bull's sister team in 2027; watch the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend live on Sky Sports F1 from November 20-22

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Racing Bulls have confirmed Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad will be retained for the 2027 Formula 1 season.

Lawson's future appeared to be in doubt earlier this month as Racing Bulls and parent team Red Bull pondered whether to replace the New Zealander with Formula 2 championship contender Nikola Tsolov.

But Lawson has retained his seat for next year, with three races left in what has comfortably been his best season in F1 so far.

The 24-year-old is the top-scoring driver from one of the grid's midfield teams and sits ninth in the Drivers' Championship on 89 points. Lawson has scored points in 15 races, three of which he spent at Red Bull in place of an injured Isack Hadjar.

Lindblad, meanwhile, has enjoyed a strong rookie season with the 19-year-old scoring 38 points.

Lawson and Lindblad's consistent points scoring has put Racing Bulls on course for their highest Constructors' Championship placing of fifth. They are 45 points ahead of Alpine and unlikely to be overhauled in the rounds that remain.

Alan Permane, Racing Bulls' team principal, said: "We're delighted to be continuing with Liam and Arvid for 2027. Both have demonstrated their ability and potential throughout the season, and we've seen the progress they've made, both individually and as a pairing.

F1 news, rumours and gossip: Formula 1 latest updates on teams, driver transfer market and contracts

Liam Lawson: Did Racing Bulls driver save his 2027 F1 seat with superb weekend at Sao Paulo GP in Brazil?

Lewis Hamilton: Ferrari's seven-time F1 world champion urges Israel to 'let the aid trucks in' to Gaza after visit to Rafah border

James Vowles: Williams boss admits team got carried away with success but says 2026 F1 season struggles are only 'a blip'

The Fast and The Curious Podcast: Vowles silences 'pressure' remarks

"I have no doubt that this is the best driver line-up for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition. Together, we have a solid foundation to build on the progress made this year, continue pushing ourselves forward and take the next step towards achieving our ambitions in 2027."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Lawson, who would almost certainly have dropped off the grid had he not been retained given the dearth of alternative seats left elsewhere, said he was "very happy" to be staying on for what will be his third full season in F1.

"We've had a brilliant season together and the team has worked very hard to produce a fast car, which I've loved driving. It feels great to be part of a historic season for the team as we continue our fight for P5 in the Constructors' Championship," said Lawson.

It's a testament to the hard work of everyone both at track, and back at the factory. I'm looking forward to carrying this moment forward with Arvid through to 2027; we're building something super positive and I'm excited by what we can achieve together."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Lindblad added: "Looking back on my first season in Formula 1, it's been a truly special year, full of new experiences and learnings since the very first pre-season test. I'd like to thank everyone at VCARB and Red Bull for their trust and support.

"I'm incredibly grateful to everyone in the team for their hard work, commitment and collaboration throughout the season, and for the strong relationships we've built along the way. I can't wait to get started next year, building on everything I've learned during my rookie season. It's set to be an exciting year, and I look forward to continuing to drive alongside Liam."

The only place officially left open on next season's 22-car grid is now at Haas, although Oliver Bearman's stay in the seat next to the newly-signed Rafael Camara is considered a formality despite the delay in re-confirming the Briton.

Bearman said recently there were "few bigger-picture things that we're working on" before the deal was tied up for 2027.

But there has been lingering speculation about Valtteri Bottas' future at Cadillac.

While the experienced Finn, like team-mate Sergio Perez, was understood to have signed a multi-year deal when he joined the start-up outfit from this season, Cadillac team principal Marcin Budkowski was coy on the team's 2027 line-up when speaking at the United States Grand Prix last month.

"In general, I think it's not something that is done in the press," said Budkowski. "It's something which will be done by official releases from the team when the time is right."

Perez was announced on a new deal to at least 2029 days later but there has, as yet, been no formal confirmation about Bottas' position.

Speaking last week in Brazil, Bottas said: "In my head, it should be okay. You know, that's what I signed up for, for the long term. And, I haven't heard anything other than that, so in my head, it should be all good."

Cadillac's test driver Colton Herta is considered the alternative option to Bottas and the American former IndyCar driver gained the final point required for a mandatory F1 superlicence in his latest practice outing for them in Brazil. Mercedes reserve driver Frederik Vesti has also been linked with the seat.

#992. Ian Holloway’s circus: why the manager’s antics are no laughing matter for fans

Swindon manager has a history of viral outbursts but fans want a united club and manager they can support

In Ian Holloway’s often madcap managerial orbit, this was simply the latest in a steady succession of eccentric outbursts. Eyes bulging as he spoke, he boomed the letter “D” and promptly stabbed himself in the chest with an imaginary dagger. Next came the letter “M” alongside a blow from another invisible knife. Finally, a “W” followed by a jab to the heart. “Dead. Man. Walking,” he declared, pausing for effect between words and briefly falling into an Oscar-worthy zombie stupor. “That’s how it feels.”

To an offbeat press conference genre containing seagulls following trawlers and self-proclaimed special ones, it was a crazy new entry worthy of its subsequent viral nature. Holloway at his finest.

The clip was widely shared, there is every chance you saw it this month. The general perception, from those of a neutral stance, was that one of football’s great characters had lost the plot. To those in the room, there was a sense that it was merely the exuberant mannerisms of a quirky manager during a tricky period. But for a large section of Swindon fans, it prompted an unamused eye roll. Here we go again. The circus tent is pitched firmly in town.

Supporting a Holloway-led club is an interesting assignment. Within weeks of taking the Swindon job two years ago on Sunday, he began constructing a hostile wall towards fans by reminding them that they could “go bowling” if they did not like his methods. Last December, he had to be restrained by his players during an altercation with a fan, while he has made a habit of telling them to “jog on” if overly vocal in their criticism.

When his side picked up a much-needed point against Walsall last week, the goalkeeping coach held him back from another confrontation with supporters. Asked about it, he goaded reporters into putting his address online so that disgruntled fans could have it out with him: “I don’t really care anymore.” So, when season‑ticket holders found their phones pinging with amused messages containing the same viral Holloway zombie clip, their lack of laughter could be forgiven.

“When you get these soundbites from Ian Holloway, outside the Swindon Town world it’s all about what a great character he is, how he says it like it is, and how it must be great to have him as manager,” says Rich Pullen, founder and co-host of the largest Swindon podcast, Loathed Strangers. “But, to a growing percentage of the Swindon community, it’s exhausting and it takes away from any of the good.

“If Swindon win, post-match he often uses it as an opportunity to have a go at the fans. It’s got to the stage where you can’t even enjoy a win without Ian Holloway being unable to hold himself from criticising fans. The easy thing to do is ignore him, but it’s almost impossible because he is everywhere. He goes viral and everyone always thinks: ‘Oh, isn’t that funny.’ Well, no. People are tired of the excess noise.”

This time last week, there was a thought that the M4 derby homecoming trip to Bristol Rovers on Saturday might hasten a possible end to Holloway’s Swindon tenure. Winless in eight games in all competitions, the discontent was not expected to abate on the preceding midweek trip to high-flying Barnet. The 3-1 victory that followed – Barnet’s first league defeat of the season – was a huge shock, thanks in no small part to the heroics of the goalkeeper, Connor Ripley, who recently declared the whole squad would “run through a brick wall” for Holloway.

Swindon might have followed it with another win, at Rovers’ Memorial Stadium, only for Matty Virtue to miss an open goal 90 seconds into the match. The forgettable goalless draw that played out at least extended Swindon’s unbeaten run to three games and kept them safely mid-table in League Two. Holloway was right to savour the improved performances, but the malaise runs deeper.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The manager had said something far more significant immediately after his viral soundbite when he continued: “The owner’s a dead man walking as well and that over‑complicates everything here.”

Even those seeking a more composed figure in Holloway’s place agree the manager is just one cog in a machine many argue has been misfiring for some time. Days after the zombie rant, the Swindon Town Supporters Trust declared the club had “lost our soul, our hope, our passion”, and urged Holloway’s comments about the Australian owner, Clem Morfuni, to “be a wake-up call”.

Since saving the club from probable administration in 2021, Morfuni has become a target of increasing fan indignation, failing to sell up and adding millions to the club’s debt. “Whilst the short-term focus may be on Ian Holloway, the bigger picture is above the role of the manager,” concluded the Trust, pointing to “a wedge with supporters so obvious that even the manager openly talks about it”.

In such a context, the uptick in form is merely one – albeit very welcome – aspect among wider misgivings. Because what fans really want is a united club and manager they can get behind; not to go jogging on.

The former Tottenham Hotspur manager has been linked with Manchester United every time the job has become available in the past few years

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Since Mauricio Pochettino arrived in English football with Southampton in January 2013, Manchester United have cycled through a dozen interim, caretaker or permanent managers, from Sir Alex Ferguson to Michael Carrick.

Even more coaches have been linked with the post, with the same names seemingly popping up every time the Old Trafford dugout is vacant.

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Mauricio Pochettino is one such manager and, according to the man himself, this was not just gossip column speculation.

The Argentine was first linked with Manchester United a decade ago, speculation that gathered pace when he met Sir Alex Ferguson for lunch in 2016, during which time he was in charge of Spurs.

“United have always shown interest,” Pochettino revealed to FourFourTwo in an interview earlier this year. “But the ideal scenario to manage there has never quite materialised.

“In any case, that lunch with Sir Alex had absolutely nothing to do with it,” he continues before explaining how the meeting came about.

“In his final season as a manager, we played a great game against United with Southampton. In the press conference after, he said we’d been the most complete opponent that United had faced.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“Through the secretary of the League Managers Association, he asked for my phone number so that we could have lunch. It was a meeting in London between colleagues – between a genius and an apprentice.

“My English wasn’t great, but Jesus Perez helped. When we asked for the bill, I wanted to take it, and so did he. We started arguing over who’d pay! “He said, “Stop Mauricio, I’m going to ask you a question. If you answer correctly, you pay. If not, I’ll pay.” I had no idea what he was going to ask.

“He said, “Name an Argentine player who scored in the 1930 World Cup final.” I replied, “Stabile.” He couldn’t believe it. The name came to me out of nowhere! In the end, I paid the bill.”

Speculation mounted again six years later in 2022, when the Red Devils would eventually go on to appoint Erik ten Hag.

“I was under contract at PSG,” Pochettino continues. “After our Champions League elimination against Real Madrid, we had no option but to make sure we secured the Ligue 1 title at least.

“United were in a hurry to announce their new manager before the end of that season because the situation had become unsustainable. I couldn’t negotiate, whereas Ajax gave Ten Hag the flexibility to do so.”

Pochettino is widely expected to replace Carrick in the dugout at Old Trafford ahead of Man United's derby with Liverpool later this month.

The Argentine coach is reported to have a $10 million break clause in his USMNT contract, which was extended over the summer following the United States' World Cup campaign.

Man United chiefs are meeting in Monaco this week to discuss the club's next steps.

#990. 'My job combines my passion for gaming and football'

Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

We're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

Growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

So a typical day for us, we'll get a new build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

So even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this. So whether that's being really analytical and having a good eye for detail and knowingwhen to pick things out and what to look for, or it could be things like timekeeping and making sure things run perfectly on time, and working with other people as well. So social skills where you have to work within a team or even lead a team.

The animation he makes, and the ball physics as well, where the ball goes off after the save."

So as much as I loved playing football, I realised quite early on I probably wasn't going to be a professionalfootballer. But I wanted to work in football and find. So at college, I studied sports science, and that's where I found my love of coaching. I did my FA Level 1 and then went on to do my FA Level 2. After I left college, I got a job at Arsenal, which was unpaid, working with them, learning how to develop my coaching skills. Which then led to me having a full-time paid job at Fulham Football Club, working with the youth teams, working with the academy teams. And then that eventually led to me going to an event. I saw an opportunity where you could apply for a job in Football Manager. It was something that naturally I was interested in, had a conversation with them, and realised it was definitely something that I would love to do.

So I went to the networking event at Kick It Out, and that was an opportunity for me to network with other football coaches, other people within the gaming industries, and have a really good insight to different jobs in football gaming. Without doing that, I wouldn't have the opportunity to meet the people at Football Manager and see a new job in gaming, which I wouldn't have beenaware of.

One of the highlights of my career so far is working on the in-and-out-of-possession system on FM 26. This is something we see in real football all the time, so being part of the team that brought that to life and brought it into the game was super cool.

Working within the football industry is a dream come true. Being able to work on something that I'm passionate about, that is played and enjoyed by millions of people, is an amazing feeling for me and an amazing opportunity that I have. And yeah, I love it.
