#926. Dalkeith to LA pays off for Porteous with Scotland recall

Ryan Porteous (second right) is happy to be back in the Scotland fold

It's been quite the journey for Ryan Porteous, literally and metaphorically.

Let's take the former first. He's gone from Dalkeith to Los Angeles in a career trajectory that started with the Hibernian Under-20s and a loan at Edinburgh City.

He then played more than 150 games for the Hibs first team - and more than 80 for Watford when he moved south of the border.

The man from Midlothian has row racked up 52 appearances for Los Angeles, the cross-town rivals of the better known LA Galaxy. A transatlantic trip that makes him smile when he remembers how it all started.

"Dalkeith, I know man. I could be the first ever, actually, to be fair," Porteous laughed when asked about his journey to California.

McTominay reveals heart treatment at World Cup

'Excited' Pocognoli on McTominay & Porteous returns and 'five leaders'

"It's some place. It's good. I stay in Pasadena. So a little bit outside the temptation zone, as I call it. I stay pretty close to the practice facility as I can't be doing with the traffic every day when I'm in and out to training."

The smile on his face, the tan on his skin and the use of the phrase "practice facility" all lend themselves to a man loving life and adapting fully to his situation.

His last Scotland cap came against Greece in March 2025 and the 27-year-old is now determined to notch up many more appearances for his country for the man who's recalled him, Sebastien Pocognoli, following an injury to Swansea City's Stephen Welsh.

"That's the same as everyone," Porteous said. "The manager is probably still figuring out who he wants to select and he's given boys an opportunity in most games.

"For me, it's all about just putting in a good representation of myself and being professional and doing what I do."

What's clearly helped him since moving to Major League Soccer in August last year is the level of forward players he's come up against, including a certain Argentine superstar who's just retired from international football.

"I'm enjoying it," Porteous said. "There's been a lot of games. It's probably something I didn't realise when I went over there, how many games there were in terms of travel and dealing with long flights, recovery times and things like that.

"That caught me off guard a little bit. It was tough, but I think, once you start getting into the swing of it, it's good.

"I think I've probably had one of my most consistent seasons over the last three or four years. The level varies, I think, between every team and every position.

Nations League: Scotland v North Macedonia

"I'm fortunate and unfortunate at the same time that the majority of the team's best players are number 10s, strikers, or wingers, so every game for me is really tough and the league's growing out there.

"You see it, there's more money getting put into it. There's bigger names coming out that, you know, aren't just coming out for retirement. I think it's a good place for me to be."

As for the aforementioned Inter Miami veteran Lionel Messi, Porteous admits: "I don't know if I enjoy being up against Messi like that, but we had a good night that night.

"But that was one where you just could never settle. We managed to get the win, so I'll take that.

"You're playing against world-class players. Even if you take Messi out of it, you're still playing against probably good Premier League forwards with the amount of money that these guys are getting paid.

"So, for me, it's playing at that level all the time and being used to coming up against these top players."

Having rediscovered his club form in Los Angeles, Porteous is now hoping to rekindle his Scotland career in Glasgow on Friday against North Macedonia.

If he can get back into the side, the man from Dalkeith might take some shifting.

#924. Bristol City give Skubala opportunity to improve form

Michael Skubala has won five of his 15 league games in charge of Bristol City

Bristol City will give under-pressure head coach Michael Skubala the chance to improve their results, particularly at home, says chief executive Charlie Boss.

The Robins have lost their past four Championship matches at Ashton Gate, culminating in last Saturday's 5-0 drubbing by Norwich City which left them in 17th place.

"The game against Norwich was a long way short of our standards and in the days that followed there have been a lot of tough and honest conversations around the building," said Boss in a video message on the club website., external

"Earlier this week the board met and we agreed to give Michael Skubala the opportunity to turn around the home form."

Skubala led Lincoln City to the League One title last season before joining Bristol City on a three-year-deal in May.

However, a run of only two wins from their past 10 matches has led to supporters voicing their concerns.

"A lot of fans made their feelings known loud and clear at Ashton Gate on Saturday and I want them to know everybody shares their frustration from the owners, the board and the players," added Boss.

"Michael Skubala more than anyone knows we need to improve - we wouldn't have made this decision if we didn't believe that together we can get through this difficult period."

Bristol City's next Championship match is at second-placed Middlesbrough on Saturday, 21 November (15:00 GMT) before home games against Wrexham and Swansea sandwich a trip to West Bromwich Albion.

#923. Daily briefing: Should old, bad science be culled from the literature?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Physicists used an algorithm to combine telescope measurements of a black hole in a different way from the original analysis.Credit: S. Lai, N. Thyagarajan, O. I. Wong and F. Diakogiannis/CSIRO

A re-evaluation of data from the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) has corroborated the findings that yielded the first-ever photo of a black hole. After the blurry image was released in 2019, sceptics argued that the circular shape seen in the shot was an artefact of the team’s image-reconstruction techniques. Independent astrophysicist Samuel Lai and his team used different methods to reanalyse the original data and their results — including new images of the black hole — largely match those of the EHT team.

The funding that voters in California have approved to earmark for immunology research — the largest ever infusion of cash for science authorized by a public vote in US history. (Nature | 5 min read)

Researchers have catalogued almost 100 proteins that get a free pass through the blood–brain barrier to maintain the health of neurons. Most of these proteins were produced in distant organs, particularly the liver. The team found that the transport of some of these proteins is disrupted in mice with a brain disease that mimics early-stage Alzheimer’s disease. The work suggests that the brain actively imports the proteins it needs to stay healthy, and that the breakdown of that transport drives the dysfunction seen in neurodegenerative disease, says neuroscientist and study co-author Andrew Yang.

The launch of the Artemis II mission to orbit the Moon produced unprecedented large-scale atmospheric disturbances, say researchers. Data from GPS receivers found that the Space Launch System — the most powerful rocket that NASA has ever built — disrupted the atmospheric layer known as the ionosphere. The GPS disruption was potentially large enough to “have a strong impact not only on self-driving cars but also on drone positioning,” says space physicist and study co-author Charles Lin.

Reference: Geophysical Research Letters preprint (not peer reviewed)

The scientific literature contains decades-old papers that detail fraudulent, unethical or merely incorrect results, but aren’t marked as such. Many of these papers are long neglected, but their digitization enables artificial-intelligence tools that summarize scientific literature on a topic to feed misinformation to a new generation. This leaves publishers to wrangle with the question of whether these historical papers should be retracted or flagged as suspect — a task that can be tricky if authors are dead, original records can’t be consulted or journals are no longer in print.

“You need a container before you can get the chemistry” that enables cellular life, says astrobiologist Bruce Damer. He’s among those researchers who favour a ‘lipid-first’ hypothesis for the origin of complex life: that the lipid membrane that corrals the cell is key to its success. Or even that bubbles of lipids, plus the chemistry they enclosed, could have propagated and evolved in a Darwinian-like way, before RNA (or DNA) arrived on the scene.

Enjoy more ideas about where we came from in Quanta Magazine’s Origins of Life Week.

Social scientists should be involved in the process of finding suitable locations for new observatories, argues anthropologist Jaco de Swart, co-principal investigator of a proposed neutrino detector to be built in the Peruvian Andes. Many suitable locations for such projects are sensitive ecological environments with cultural significance for Indigenous communities. Social scientists can help to integrate environmental care into these projects and build relationships with local and Indigenous stakeholders. “To build scientific infrastructure that is responsible, just and resilient, humanities scholars must have leadership roles from the start,” de Swart writes.

Appearing in the Jurassic Park franchise is the strongest predictor of a dinosaur species’ popularity, according to new research — an example of the ‘blockbuster effect’. The media should leverage this effect to put a spotlight on endangered species, says zoologist Pâmela Lima. (Science | 7 min read)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03675-y

The Kangaroo is a multiple-choice mathematics challenge attempted by more than seven million children in around 120 countries, just for fun. The Guardian’s maths-puzzle-master Alex Bellos shared a Kangaroo question from the 2024 event that should be accessible to skilled secondary-school students — so Briefing readers will certainly be good to have a go. The answer is here.

Did you manage to tame the Kangaroo? Let me know — along with any other feedback on this newsletter — at briefing@nature.com.

#922. JULES BREACH: Brighton's brilliant start has fans believing of silverware and challenging for the Champions League

The TNT Sports presenter and Brighton fan on why the Seagulls should dare to dream

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This season, I think I’ve lost count of the amount of times someone has come up to me and said, “Brighton are in the title race, aren’t they?” Whether they’ve been joking or not, the fact they’ve included the club in the conversation is bonkers. We’ve enjoyed the adulation – it was deserved after an impressive run of results to start the season.

Brighton have begun the campaign as entertainers. Fabian Hurzeler has them free-scoring, upsetting the Premier League champions and playing an attacking brand of football that’s fun to watch.

Most Albion fans have been realistic that mounting a title challenge is one step too far. What does feel possible though, and it still feels crazy that I’m even writing this, is that there’s probably never been a better opportunity to challenge for a Champions League place – madness for a club that only experienced European football for the first time in its history in 2023.

On top of the Seagulls’ great start, some of the usual contenders for the Champions League places didn’t really get going early on. Manchester United and Spurs both struggled, Liverpool and Chelsea were still settling under new managers, and Manchester City have been at risk of being hit with sanctions this term. If ever there was a season where a disruptor could break into those qualification spots, it’s this one. Brighton will be one of the favourites to do it.

I’ll be honest and admit that before a ball was even kicked, I was nervous about this season. As fans, we’re used to losing key players and coping pretty well, but to lose the spine of Jan Paul van Hecke, Carlos Baleba and Danny Welbeck all in the same window was a big blow. Joao Pedro was sold the summer before, and losing both the Brazilian and Welbeck in successive summers without an experienced replacement felt risky.

Scoring goals was a huge concern, but I’ve been proven completely wrong. Again. The club have shown once more that they’re not just one step ahead of everyone else, but two. They had their best ever start to a top-flight season, and over the first seven league games of the campaign, only Barcelona and Bayern Munich had scored more among Europe’s top five leagues.

Brighton consistently find hidden gems. It’s a testament to their recruitment policy and they appear to have done it again with a number of players. The club don’t mind marketing themselves as one that helps a player progress and allows them to leave if a big offer arises, and their culture provides young talent a platform to thrive without too much pressure.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Greek teenage striker Charalampos Kostoulas looks like one of the best young players in the league and is key to Hurzeler’s aggressive press. Also just 19 years old, no-one expected Luka Vuskovic to replace Van Hecke so well. They are two young players who are flourishing in a team that also has plenty of experience in captain Lewis Dunk and Pascal Gross to give it the right balance.

Brighton’s stand-out performer has been 35-year-old Gross, who returned to the club in a genius January move after a season-and-a-half at Borussia Dortmund. His workrate, and goal and assist output had already given him legendary status at the Amex, but he’s been on another level and is clearly enjoying his football more than ever.

There have already been a handful of memorable results, including the comeback win at Old Trafford, a 3-0 victory at home to Arsenal and a 5-0 thrashing of rivals Crystal Palace, which included that halfway line goal from Diego Gomez. It will go down as one of the all-time great Premier League strikes and summed up the confidence Brighton are playing with.

The challenge now is to compete consistently and stay in this crazy conversation as long as possible. As fans, we always expect a bad run just around the corner, but this season could be special. The club are Conference League favourites, and supporters are desperate to see a first major trophy.

Football is there to make us believe and Brighton fans will continue to dream after the start we’ve seen. There may never be a better opportunity to break into the Champions League than now, but lifting that first piece of silverware surely has to be a priority.

Jules Breach is a broadcast journalist who has lead presenting roles for TNT Sport, Channel 4, ITV, and Premier League Productions. Jules hosted BT Sport’s live flagship football show Score and also presents live Premier League, Europa League and Champions League matches. Jules is the lead presenter for Channel 4’s coverage of the England games and also hosts ITV’s EFL Highlights show. Jules presents worldwide coverage for Premier League Productions and away from work is a passionate Brighton fan.

#920. Sisters in Sweat: how a former Spurs player got 20,000 Indian women into sport

A dinner-party question, a Sunday kickabout and an idea that snowballed. Nine years on, Tanvie Hans and Swetha Subbiah have taken sporting sisterhood to 10 cities

On a breezy evening in 2017, as conversations flowed and so did the drinks at a dinner party, Tanvie Hans was asked an all-too-familiar question at the table: “Hey, can you teach me how to play football?”

For the Indian-born British footballer, who played professionally in England, it was an easy yes.

After a little planning and some back-and-forth messages 17 women – mostly friends and acquaintances – turned up for Hans’ first football lesson on a Sunday morning in the southern Indian metropolis of Bengaluru, eager to discover the joy of the sport.

Nine years on from that impromptu football session, the group has grown into a community of 20,000 women across India. They may not be sisters by blood, but they are the Sisters in Sweat. Co-founded by Hans and the performance coach Swetha Subbiah, Sisters in Sweat is India’s largest women-first sports community, built to help women move more, play more and connect through a variety of sports.

From Chandigarh in the north to Chennai in the south, the initiative now spans 10 Indian cities, with football among its most popular offerings. “It wasn’t something that Swetha and I sat down to plan or even recognised was a gap in the market,” Hans, a former Tottenham and Fulham midfielder, tells Moving the Goalposts.

“But the moment we started these sessions they became successful and the community kept growing organically. That’s when we recognised that we were catering to an audience that is not being catered to in this way. And who better to do it than two women who are experts in the field?”

At Sisters in Sweat, coach-led football sessions are conducted two to three times a week, with participants free to choose between beginner and intermediate sessions, depending on their level of ability. The entry fee starts at about 300 Indian rupees – just under £2.50 – and women of all ages are welcome. You could be trying football for the first time, getting back to it or simply looking for a fun way to stay active.

The format is pretty simple, and the same one Hans and Subbiah used at their first gathering in 2017. The session begins with a quick huddle; everyone introduces themselves and the coach explains what to expect in the next 90 minutes. A warm-up follows before partner or group drills help break the ice within the group, which often features new faces every week. There is music playing in the background to create a celebratory mood and the session ends with a quick and easy 30-minute game of football.

A first-time participant often leaves with a smile, having ticked off a workout while meeting a bunch of strangers who they can now call friends. “You feel like, ‘Oh, I can actually play football and want to get better. I can’t wait to come back for the next session’,” Hans says. “Honestly, just being at the session opens doors for connection. It happens very naturally, and by the end of 90 minutes, you feel you belong here.”

Beyond nurturing new connections, Sisters in Sweat offers women something increasingly rare in India’s densely populated tier 1 cities: access to third spaces where they can show up and move their bodies without fear of judgment or safety concerns. With India’s fitness market projected to grow from $12.3bn (£9.2bn) in 2024 to $23.2bn by 2030 – an 88.6% increase over six years – Sisters in Sweat’s growth and expansion reflect the broader industry trend.

“My cousin, who is from the UK, was actively involved in our Sisters in Sweat sessions while she was in India on holiday. But after she returned to the UK, she wasn’t able to find a community like that,” Subbiah says. “I have heard the same thing from friends in Singapore and other countries. So, I think we, in many ways, have been the first movers to identify this.”

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

At the heart of Sisters in Sweat’s aim is to fill the gaping hole left by Indian women dropping out of sport, especially after school or college. In the country’s deeply patriarchal social structure, many women are often discouraged from venturing outdoors alone or playing sport recreationally. For many, having the freedom to stay out late at night is a distant dream or a luxury, at best.

“Once a woman leaves her role as a student, she moves on to her next role in life, which is typically becoming a wife,” Subbiah, who has been a Nike coach for over a decade, says. “Then she takes on all the household duties. Add a kid into the mix, and her personal time is minimised.

“There is also immense pressure on a lot of Indian women not to go out or play outdoors because they could catch a tan and look less appealing. A lot of the work we’ve done is to push past these social constructs and say, “Get a tan, it’s beautiful. Come out and play with us, you’ll feel great.”

#918. Beirne captains strong Ireland selection vs Fiji as Gibson-Park returns

Andy Farrell's Ireland host Fiji at Aviva Stadium, Dublin on Saturday in Nations Championship (8.10pm); team selection shows seven changes to thumping win vs Argentina as Jamison Gibson-Park, Tommy O'Brien, Bundee Aki, Jamie Osborne, Ronan Kelleher, James Ryan, Josh van der Flier come in

Tadhg Beirne will captain a strong Ireland selection vs Fiji in the Nations Championship on Saturday, despite head coach Andy Farrell making seven changes.

Two of those changes are enforced as hooker Dan Sheehan (concussion) and No 8 Sean Jansen (knee) were ruled out, but several other injury concerns have been allayed.

Indeed, wing Rob Baloucoune is fit to start again, as is Mack Hansen despite an ankle knock - the latter shifting to full-back with Hugo Keenan rested and Tommy O'Brien brought into the back-three.

Josh van der Flier is also fit despite his own ankle complaint, starting at openside flanker with Nick Timoney shifting to No 8 in the absence of Jansen, Jack Conan and Caelan Doris due to injury.

Experienced scrum-half Jamison Gibson-Park returns to the starting XV, with Craig Casey dropping down to the bench.

Elsewhere, there is a new-look midfield with Jamie Osborne and Bundee Aki starting at centre. Stuart McCloskey moves to the bench, while Robbie Henshaw drops out of the matchday squad.

Sam Prendergast partners Gibson-Park at half-back, while Ronan Kelleher replaces Sheehan at hooker to form a front-row alongside Andrew Porter and Tadhg Furlong.

James Ryan is promoted from the bench to start in place of the rested Joe McCarthy, with Ryan Baird completing the back-row alongside Van der Flier and Timoney.

On the bench, uncapped Ulster back-row James McNabney is in line for his Test debut.

Ireland: 15 Mack Hansen, 14 Robert Baloucoune, 13 Jamie Osborne, 12 Bundee Aki, 11 Tommy O'Brien, 10 Sam Prendergast, 9 Jamison Gibson-Park; 1 Andrew Porter, 2 Ronan Kelleher, 3 Tadhg Furlong, 4 James Ryan, 5 Tadhg Beirne, 6 Ryan Baird, 7 Josh van der Flier, 8 Nick Timoney.

Replacements: 16 Tom Stewart, 17 Tom O'Toole, 18 Sam Illo, 19 Darragh Murray, 20 James McNabney, 21 Craig Casey, 22 Ciaran Frawley, 23 Stuart McCloskey.

#914. Daveigh Chase Was Found in Car With Meth Pipe Days Before Death

Child actress Daveigh Chase was found in a car “with complaints of headache, weakness, confusion” days before her death, per the Los Angeles Medical Examiner.

More details have come to light about Daveigh Chase’s heartbreaking final days.

Before the Lilo & Stitch star died at 35 on June 16, she was found in the back of a car and subsequently hospitalized for various illnesses, the Los Angeles Medical Examiner confirmed to Us Weekly Nov. 10.

On June 4, the child star “was found in the back seat of a vehicle with complaints of headache, weakness, confusion, right thumb pain and a meth pipe nearby” just eight days before her death, the medical examiner told the outlet. She was then transported to a hospital by ambulance.

She was admitted with “advanced HIV/AIDS with wasting” and “cryptococcus without meningitis,” according to the medical examiner’s investigation report obtained by the outlet.

Wasting is a condition in which a person involuntarily loses at least 10 percent of their body weight, including muscle mass and fat, according to the National Cancer Institute. It often affects people with severe chronic conditions, per the Cleveland Clinic.

Meanwhile, Cryptococcus is an illness that stems from a fungal infection in the body, per the Cleveland Clinic, which noted that people with compromised immune systems—such as those with HIV/AIDS—are at a higher risk of experiencing the illness.

In addition to an infection in her thumb, Chase (real name Daveigh Schwallier) was also diagnosed with MRSA, or Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection, at the hospital, a type of staph bacteria “that's become resistant to many of the antibiotics used to treat ordinary staph infections,” according to the Mayo Clinic.

The report also noted that toxicological screenings found Chase positive for “methamphetamine and fentanyl” in her system.

Chase had a “history of advanced and untreated HIV/AIDS and drug use,” the report noted, adding that her health had declined until her death.

The Donnie Darko actress died on June 16 from an acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)-related illness, with substance abuse considered a "significant condition" contributing to her death, according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records viewed by E! News.

She died in the hospital, per the records, with officials listing her manner of death as natural.

Following her passing, Chase’s boyfriend Roy Hernandez shared additional insight into the personal struggles she experienced in the lead-up to her death.

"My girlfriend has always been a light in my life," he wrote on his GoFundMe. "Many people know her as a talented childhood actor from Lilo & Stitch, Spirited Away, and Donnie Darko. But behind the scenes, she's faced more than her share of hardship."

"After a difficult childhood and a painful falling out with her family, Daveigh was bullied and struggled to find safety and happiness in downtown LA," he continued. "When we met, I promised to protect her and give her the love and comfort she deserved. Together, we found moments of happiness and hope."

#912. Shrewsbury 'hit all the boxes' for new owners - Friedel

Shrewsbury Town's new sporting director Brad Friedel's previous coaching experience is chiefly at international level

Shrewsbury Town's new sporting director Brad Friedel says the League Two club are the perfect project for the new American owners following a Europe-wide search.

Miami-based Scott Davidson's Biscayne ST LLC consortium, of which Friedel is part, completed their majority takeover on Monday, buying 87.4% of the shares, allowing long-time owner Roland Wycherley to relinquish control after 30 years.

"Scott and I met through friends in Miami and through the love of football, nothing more or less," former USA goalkeeper Friedel told BBC Radio Shropshire in an exclusive interview.

"As we got to know each other, our thoughts on business and football aligned. We got to the point where we said let's try to find a club which fits a whole bunch of criteria."

Friedel group completes Shrewsbury Town takeover

"We looked in Turkey, Poland, Portugal and Holland but, at the clubs we were looking, something didn't align for one reason or another. A lot of it came down to 'Did we think our group can help the football club?' We want to bring the town firmly behind the club."

Wycherley first announced his plans to find a successor five years ago and Friedel says, with Davidson already being a majority shareholder of Edinburgh-based The Spartans in Scottish League Two, they wanted a club they could take forward.

"The one-town club really appealed. We want to integrate the club even more into the town than it is now. When you look at the investment going into the EFL, the foreign investment, there's a reason for it. There's no better place for football than the United Kingdom.

"Once we decided our group would be best suited to the UK market, Shrewsbury hit all the boxes. But also what we feel we can deliver towards the club and the town."

Shrewsbury takeover in 'final stages' - Wycherley

As a player, Friedel spent the majority of his club career in the Premier League with Liverpool, Blackburn Rovers, Aston Villa and Tottenham Hotspur, but the 55-year-old is unfazed about taking his first sporting director role in England's fourth tier.

"I don't look at football anymore as I would only take a job in the Premier League or the Champions League," he said. "One of my most enjoyable jobs post-playing career was being head coach of the US men's under-19 national team and most of those players weren't even professional.

"I look at football opportunities with different projects. The upside, if you get it right in English football, is there is such a buzz for me out of it, so I don't look at this as an EFL League Two club, I look at is as another incredible project with incredible people."

Shrewsbury finished 10 points clear of relegation in League Two last season, having appointed former player Gavin Cowan as head coach in January to help steer them clear of a drop into the National League - and Friedel intends to work closely with him.

"I'm moving over here," he added. "I'll be there day-to-day so this is not a situation where you'll see me every now and then at the club. I'm not here for the short term.

"It'll be a collaboration. The way we see football being successful is you have to have roles and structure but you can't have dictators. Gavin and I will be around each other every day. I'll be at training every day.

"It's a group effort. If we're successful it will have nothing to do with just what I do or Scott does or Gavin does. It's everybody on and off the field who has to pull their weight for us to be successful."

One area the new owners intend to concentrate on is recruitment - and Friedel is already at work identifying potential new signings.

"I'm very much data driven but I'd never sign a player just on data as there are so many different elements to signing a player," he said.

"What data does is speed up the process. We have our own customised platform and we'll be bringing in other individuals to help with the recruitment process. We'll collaborate with Gavin and extend a much wider net around the globe.

"We will reach out to many parts of the world that have not been previously by Shrewsbury Town. We're excited about bringing this recruitment department in. It's something that's already in place. They're here and we're already working."

This is a second season in League Two for Shrewsbury, whose 10-season stay in League One ended in 2025.

They last played in the second tier in 1989 but Friedel is not ruling out the club returning to that level at some point in the future.

"Everything is possible," he said. "You've got to dream but let's take one thing at a time. We want to come in and take this step-by-step.

"We want to be possible promotion contenders, whether it's this season or next. That's our aim. If we're fortunate enough to get up into League One we'll try to do it again and, if we get up into the Championship, that's another formidable task.

"We want to baby-step this. First stability, structure and make sure we're providing the resources needed for the first-team staff, for the players to be successful and for the academy to be successful and then see where we go."

#911. How Nathan Fielder Got Amanda Seyfried to Join You Can See Everything

In their first open conversation about You Can See Everything, Amanda Seyfried, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim detailed how The Dropout star joined the Elizabeth Holmes documentary.

Amanda Seyfried actually didn’t see everything.

In her first conversation about her participation in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim new documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, You Can See Everything, The Dropout alum revealed she signed onto the project without consulting her team.

“When you said you had 90 minutes of footage for me to see and help you work through, I was like, ‘Oh, he just wants some advice,’” Seyfried recalled of her earliest conversations with Fielder—with whom she was connected through Emma Stone—in a joint interview alongside Oppenheim for Rolling Stone published Nov. 11. “He just wants us to know about my experience playing her and researching her and going into the mind of that quote-unquote character I portrayed.’”

However, while Seyfried had previously said she’d never portray the disgraced Theranos founder after the limited series, Fielder and Oppenheim’s film, which released in theaters in early November, was too inspiring to pass up.

“After the Zoom, I was totally game to do whatever you needed,” she continued. “It was just your energy [that persuaded me], and how much time you had spent [on this project], and that nobody knew this was happening.”

But while Fielder has earned a reputation for truly shocking projects, Seyfried “wasn’t nervous” to work with The Rehearsal creator.

“There was no protection,” the 40-year-old—who acknowledged she had to remind herself to put on mascara before they began filming for the first time—continued. “There was no advocate for me. I just felt like I was totally game because I was so invested in what you were doing and already had this strange level of trust in you guys.”

Still, Seyfried admitted that as her involvement in the project grew—the Mean Girls alum ended up participating in reenactments as Holmes alongside Christopher Abbott, who played Holmes’ husband Billy Evans, as well as appearing as herself—she weighed “a lot of risk” in her mind.

In fact, Fielder emphasized that Seyfried had “no approval” over the scripts or dialogue in the film to ensure its documentary standard.

“There was always this vibration of risk and that sensation of: Am I going to destroy my career in some way?” the Mamma Mia star continued. “Am I going to get entangled in this, like, wasp’s nest with Billy? Am I gonna say the wrong thing? Am I gonna perpetuate negativity for her?”

But now that the project has been out in the world for nearly a month, Seyfried clarified, “I don’t regret it at all.”

You Can See Everything is now in theaters. For more about those involved in the Theranos scandal, keep reading…

Theranos officially dissolved in September 2018, three months after founder Elizabeth Holmes and company president Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani were indicted on federal wire fraud charges for luring investors with the promise of a blood-testing technology that was not ready to bring to the masses.

While awaiting trial, Holmes and partner Billy Evans welcomed son William in July 2021.

She pleaded not guilty to all charges, but was convicted in January 2022 of one count of conspiracy to defraud investors, plus three wire fraud counts tied to specific investors, and subsequently sentenced to 11 years in prison.

Holmes gave birth to daughter Invicta in February 2023. In her first prison interview, she told People in 2025, "I always wanted to be a mother. I truly did not think I would ever be convicted or found guilty.”

A month before she was due to begin serving her time, Holmes and Evans opened up their San Diego, Calif., rental to Nathan Fielder and a small documentary crew. The result, You Can See Everything, is in theaters Oct. 16, 2026.

Holmes reported to minimum-security Federal Prison Camp, Bryan in Texas on May 30, 2023. She's scheduled to be transferred to a halfway house in August 2027.

“I was silenced for a long time," Holmes wrote in a Sept. 27 X post. “And then imprisoned. I am fighting to prove my innocence and come home to my babies and the love of my life."

Balwani, who was in a romantic relationship with Holmes while he was a Theranos executive, also pleaded not guilty on all counts.

"He did not defraud Theranos investors, who were among the most sophisticated in the world,"his lawyer told Vanity Fair in 2018. "He did not defraud consumers, but instead worked tirelessly to empower them with access to their own health information."

Balwani was convicted of 10 counts of wire fraud and two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud in July 2022 and sentenced to 12 years and 11 months in federal prison, with U.S. Attorney Stephanie M. Hinds stating he "valued business success and personal wealth far more than patient safety."

The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals upheld his conviction and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear the case in October 2026.

Balwani is incarcerated at Federal Correctional Institution, Lompoc II, a low-security facility in California.

A grandson of former Secretary of State George Shultz, one of Theranos' most prominent board members, Tyler Shultz interned at the company in 2013 and then was hired full-time as a research engineer.

He has since become a sought-after public speaker on corporate ethics and his experience blowing the whistle on Theranos' mismanagement and internal malpractice.

Shultz founded the health diagnostics company Flux Biosciences in 2017 and is now a venture partner at Verge HealthlTech Fund, according to Linked In.

When Holmes was convicted of fraud, he told NPR in 2022, "All of a sudden, it was just a weight was lifted. It's over. I can't believe it's over."

He was staying with his parents when his wife texted him the verdict. And then, Shultz shared, "My family said, 'Come on down we're popping champagne. We're celebrating.'"

Lab associate Erika Cheung was also key in exposing wrongdoing at Theranos following her resignation after seven months at the company.

"It wasn't that we were trying to be alarmist or sabotage [Holmes] or that, as she thought, we were trying to come after her and had some vendetta against her," Cheung told the Los Angeles Times in 2019. "I think we were all motivated by the fact that you can't endanger the life of patients. This is healthcare."

By then, the UC Berkeley grad had moved to Hong Kong and was a program director at Betatron, a technology accelerator for founders and start-ups.

She has since returned to the U.S., where she runs Ethics in Entrepreneurship, a nonprofit she founded in 2019 that also counts Shultz as an advisor.

Calling herself and Shultz "lucky in a certain way," Cheung told the Times, "It was a big relief once the company went under that we did come out of this OK and it didn’t damage our careers."

Holmes poached Ana Arriola, who helped conceive the original iPhone, from Apple to be her chief design architect—part of her vision to help give her blood-testing device, the Edison, a sleek look.

Far more culturally impactful: Arriola told Holmes all about Steve Jobs' Issey Miyaki black turtlenecks.

As Arriola put it on ABC News' The Dropout podcast, "And the rest is couture history."

She joined Theranos in 2007 and left after four months, concerned that the Edison's as-yet unreliable results could affect the treatment for cancer patients who had submitted blood samples.

Holmes "gave me an ultimatum," Arriola said, "suppress it and continue on business as usual or I said I was resigning."

After Theranos, Arriola worked for companies including Sony, Samsung and Microsoft. She has since married, become a mom and moved to Japan, where, according to LinkedIn, she is an executive advisor for venture studio OrionsWave in Tokyo, as well as strategic advisor and director at architecture and design firm OEO Studio.

As chief software technology officer at Apple, Avie Tevanian led the team that developed Mac OS before leaving in 2006 and subsequently joining Theranos' board of directors after—like everyone else—being impressed by Holmes.

"I think what she didn't expect was that I would actually ask a lot of questions," Tevanian said in The Dropout, "and that if things weren't going as they should be going that I would ask tough questions." When he told the board he would only stay on if Holmes was replaced as CEO by someone more qualified, a fellow member suggested he help them help Holmes, or resign.

"I was done with Theranos," Tevanian told ABC News' Rebecca Jarvis. "I had seen so many things that were bad go on. I would never expect anyone would behave the way that she behaved as a CEO. And believe me, I worked for Steve Jobs. I saw some crazy things. But Elizabeth took it to a new level."

Tevanian is a co-founder of NextEquity Partners.

There was at least one person who told Holmes that what she was trying to do with the Edison was impossible: Stanford professor of medicine Dr. Phyllis Gardner.

Holmes first shared her blood test idea when she was a freshman. And when the clinical pharmacologist told her it would never work, Holmes "just kind of blinked her eyes and nodded, and left," Gardner said on The Dropout. "It was just a 19-year-old talking who'd taken one course in microfluidics, and she thought she was gonna make something of it."

Also a former senior associate dean at Stanford University School of Medicine, Gardner died Sept. 10, 2025, at the age of 75.

“Integrity ran through everything she did,” her husband, Dr. Andrew Perlman, told the Stanford Medicine News Center. “She couldn’t abide dishonesty in science or in people.”

The former Senior Associate Dean for Faculty & Academic Affairs at Stanford's School of Engineering was a mentor to Holmes and Theranos' first board member. He compared the company's founder to the "Mozarts and the Beethovens and the Newtons, the Lavoisiers and the Einsteins and the da Vincis."

As he explained to Bloomberg Businessweek, per ABC News, "These people who become scientists and artists and musicians, I think, possess a very special capability. It was becoming more and more clear to me that she had it. I was in the presence of somebody who was unlike anything that I had seen before."

Robertson remains a professor emeritus of chemical engineering at Stanford.

#910. From W-M to the No 10, shirt numbers tell a story of football’s tactical evolution

In the days before squad numbers, the number on a shirt was an indicator of position, as well as the attributes a player was supposed to demonstrate

Ultimate 1-50: check out our complete list of players

Numbers have a fascination. The No 10 is revered almost everywhere, but perhaps most especially in Argentina, where it denotes the playmaker, the enganche, the quasi-mythical figure who links the front and back of the team. Liverpool and Manchester United have reasons to celebrate their No 7. Ajax retired No 14 for Johan Cruyff, Milan their No 3 and No 6 for Paolo Maldini and Franco Baresi respectively and Birmingham their 22 for Jude Bellingham as gestures of respect for their abilities. Other numbers have been retired to mark premature deaths: the No 20 at Liverpool for Diogo Jota, the No 23 at Manchester City for Marc-Vivian Foé, the 21 at Espanyol for Daniel Jarque.

But numbers are not just about individuals. In the days before squad numbers, the number on a shirt was an indicator of position, and the expectations of particular numbers in particular cultures, as well as the attributes a player in that shirt was supposed to demonstrate, themselves tell a story of tactical evolution.

The earliest evidence of teams wearing numbered shirts seems to be in a game between the Australian sides Sydney Leichhardt and HSM Powerful in 1911. The University of Chicago’s American football team wore squad numbers in 1913. There were experiments with numbers on sleeves in baseball from 1916. There were isolated efforts with numbered shirts in the American Soccer League, which began in 1923, and, especially, in the USA’s Challenge Cup. Various touring sides began to experiment with numbered shirts through the 1920s and, in August 1928, on the opening day of the English league season, two games featured numbers. Chelsea’s outfielders wore 2-11 in their Second Division game against Swansea, while Sheffield Wednesday wore 1-11 and Arsenal 12-22 in a First Division clash at Hillsborough.

Similarly, 1-22 numbering was used in the 1933 FA Cup final, in part because Everton and Manchester City were forced to wear change kits due to a colour clash, although the presence of the touring West Indies cricket side, who were not expected to be familiar with the individual players, was also cited. It wasn’t until June 1939, though, that the Football League took a vote to introduce squad numbers. It passed 24-20, and it was decided both teams should wear 1-11, but in strict order, as though the formation had been laid out on a page with the goalkeeper at the top.

This was complicated by the fact that, although almost every team by that stage had responded to the 1925 change in the offside law by adopting the W-M formation (a 3-2-2-3), there was still a belief that the “right” way to play was a 2-3-5. Thus the goalkeeper wore No 1, the right-back No 2, the left-back No 3, the right-half No 4, the centre-half No 5 and so on up to the centre-forward in No 9, the inside-left in No 10 and the left-winger in No 11. In practice, though, the centre-half (5), played between the full-backs (2 and 3) while the inside-forwards (8 and 10) played deeper than the wingers and centre-forward (7, 9 and 11).

Numbers rapidly became sacrosanct. When Hungary came to Wembley in 1953 and became the first foreign side to beat England at the national stadium, they provoked consternation because they were “incorrectly” numbered. The centre-back Mihaly Lantos wore No 4. The midfield creator Jozsef Bozsik wore No 5. Most bafflingly of all, Nandor Hidegkuti, the No 9, didn’t play as a centre-forward but created from midfield. What was Harry Johnston, England’s hapless centre-half, to do? Convention said he, the No 5, should pick up the No 9, but if he did that he left a huge hole in the back line. And if he did not, Hidegkuti was free to pick England apart.

The introspection provoked by that defeat led within a decade or so to a number of leading English teams adopting a back four, usually by withdrawing the left-half (the No 6) into the defensive line. As Alf Ramsey’s 1966 World Cup winners showed the value of packing midfield, so the wingers dropped back, leaving a 4-4-2 that lined up: 1; 2, 5, 6, 3; 7, 4, 8, 11; 9, 10. Within that, the No 4 would usually be the more defensive of the two central midfielders, while the No 10 retained some of the qualities of the inside-left, which is to say he tended to be the smaller, more creative forward alongside a big, physical number No 9.

Other countries, though, followed a different path. In Argentina, for instance, there had been no sudden shift to W-M in the late 1920s but, at River Plate in the late 1930s, the right-half Norberto Yácono, nicknamed “the Stamp” for his tight marking, would pick up the opposing creator. As other teams followed the principle, the number No 4 became a de facto third back, but operating on the right. No 4 remains the standard number for an Argentinian right-back, as exemplified by Javier Zanetti, for whom Inter retired the shirt. When Argentina switched to a back four after the humiliation of the 6-1 defeat to Czechoslovakia at the 1958 World Cup, the left-half fell into the back line, so a standard Argentinian back four would read: 4, 2, 6, 3. The No 5 remained as the caudillo in midfield, almost as venerated as the No 10 in the form of Antonio Rattín, Américo Gallego and Javier Mascherano.

In Brazil, though, there had been no widespread conversion of the right-half into a right-back, and so when the back four was adopted, the wing-halves simply dropped either side of the full-backs, leaving a standard back four as: 4, 2, 3, 6. The great right-back Carlos Alberto, for instance, wore No 4 at the 1970 World Cup, while the left-back Roberto Carlos tended to wear No 6. When, at Flamengo in the 1940s, Flávio Costa tipped the midfield square of Dori Kürschner’s W-M to create his diagonal, a major step towards 4-2-4, the No 5 became the more defensive central midfielder – leading to players such as Clodoaldo, Mauro Silva and Casemiro wearing the shirt for the national team – while the inside-left, the No 10, became the most creative midfielder.

In other countries, other conventions emerged. It was in the Netherlands and West Germany that the standard delineations of the expectations on midfielders in a 4-3-3 emerged. The No 6 would be the deep-lying player, the No 10 would be the creator, and the No 8 would be a box-to-box player shuttling between them. Or in France, where a five-man bench from which a manger could use two substitutes was adopted in 1976, it became standard for the reserve goalkeeper to wear No 16. Many goalkeepers in the Francophone world gained their first experience wearing No 16 and so favoured it when squad numbers were introduced: that’s why Fabian Barthez wore No 16 at the 1998 World Cup and Cameroon’s Thomas N’Kono wore it in 1990.

Numbers now are often a matter of personal choice and of brand-building. In a squad system, players can take on a familiar number and hope to embody its spirit, or try to make a more obscure number their own, as Johan Cruyff did with the No 14 more than half a century ago.

Numbers have a past, and they tell a story. Nobody on the Football League committee that narrowly voted to mandate squad numbers in 1939 would have considered the possibility, but in numbers are written the deep history of a country’s tactical development.

#909. Greaves 'excited' to face Littler at Grand Slam of Darts

Beau Greaves will face Luke Littler this Saturday at the Grand Slam of Darts as the pair have been drawn in the same group as each other; watch the Grand Slam of Darts from this Saturday at 1pm and 7pm, live on Sky Sports

Sports Journalist @NigelCJourno

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Beau Greaves says she is "excited" to face Luke Littler on the opening day of the Grand Slam of Darts this weekend.

Greaves has been drawn in the same group as Littler and Dutch player Niels Zonneveld with only the top player from each group progressing to the knockout stages.

Littler and Greaves will meet for the first time since the latter beat the world champion at the World Youth Championship 12 months ago in Saturday's night's Grand Slam of Darts session, which begins at 7pm, live on Sky Sports.

"I think he's the best [player in the world] in my eyes, I think he's fantastic to watch, he's been amazing, so I always imagine he's going to play really well," said Greaves.

"I don't want to go in there thinking, 'oh he's not on form', or he's struggling, because then I would just be terrible, so I've got to go in there thinking 'he's going to absolutely smash me', and just play my game, and try and take any chance I can, and just enjoy it.

"I think it's going to be a good game just to watch, and just to be a part of it is special. I look forward to playing it."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Greaves has played in the last three Grand Slam of Darts and won two matches but is yet to get out of the group stages.

The 22-year-old narrowly lost to Michael van Gerwen and Gary Anderson, despite averaging over 100, last year and is hoping to perform well on the big stage once again.

"I played decent at the Grand Slam last year. I have good moments, but I just don't do it consistently enough," she said.

"It's something that, if I am going to do really well in the sport, I'm going to have to get better at. It's a challenge for me, but I look forward to it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I always look forward to kind of getting better and improving. I'm aware that obviously I'm not up to that standard as I do play on the floor, but it's just a work in progress at the minute, I would call it.

"But I'm just trying to look forward to everything rather than dread anything and obviously look forward to playing on stage rather than think I'd rather play on the floor. So, I'm just trying to switch it around a little bit."

The Grand Slam has expanded this year from 32 to 48 players and sees 16 groups of three, rather than four players in a group.

The format adds jeopardy as anybody who loses their opening match will be under serious pressure and could be eliminated, even if they win their second match.

"I didn't know. I didn't have a clue that there was only three in the group! I don't know why they've done it really. It didn't make much sense to me, but again, I don't really know," said Greaves.

"It's just odd, but I suppose you've still got to do well to win your group regardless but it's different, I was a bit shocked."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Greaves says she has felt "relaxed" when playing Littler in the past and is "excited" to face the world No 1, who has won the last two Grand Slam of Darts titles.

"I know Luke's loads better than me, but I kind of have to at least convince myself I can win," she said.

"I can't go up there wanting to get beat but I know it's obviously, he's 10 times better than me, but strange to think about if you get beat.

"Luke Littler is the heavy favourite to come through that group obviously, so it's strange, but there is a big jump in prize money if you finish second or third, so there's still a little bit to play for on the ranking, so just trying to not think about it and just try and enjoy every game, and try and do my best."

Watch the Grand Slam of Darts from this Saturday until Sunday, November 22 live on Sky Sports. Stream darts and more through NOW with no contract.

#907. VisionQuest Finale Reveals Fate of Marvel Character Before Doomsday

VisionQuest's finale brought love, loss, acceptance and the return of a very beloved Marvel character ahead of Avengers: Doomsday, which premieres Dec. 18.

Warning: This story contains spoilers for VisionQuest season one, episode eight.

More than love is persevering ahead of Avengers: Doomsday.

After the VisionQuest finale reunited Vision (Paul Bettany) and sons Tommy Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica) and Billy Maximoff (Joe Locke) to defeat a grieving Ultron (James Spader) from his attempt to wipe out humanity, Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen) teased her return to the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

The second post-credit scene from the Nov. 11 episode begins with a flashback to Wanda, a.k.a. the Scarlet Witch—who was drowning in grief and corrupted by the Darkhold's dark magic after losing Vision and her sons in WandaVision—burying herself in rubble at the end of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.

Her moment of redemption followed the wake of destruction after she tried to kidnap another version of her sons—who disappeared after she let go of her projected version of Westview—when she brought down the temple at Mount Wundagore, wiping out every copy of the Darkhold across the multiverse.

But Dr. Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) has other plans for Wanda. As he lifted debris from her lifeless body, he proclaimed, "Scarlet Witch, awaken. Your power will be mine."

Worlds collide in Doomsday—premiering Dec. 18—with many of the OG Avengers (minus Downey's late Iron Man), Black Panther's Wakandans, the Fantastic Four and the X-Men uniting to face Dr. Doom's existential threat to the multiverse.

It was unclear whether Wanda would also return before the post-credit scene but Vision did tell Tommy at the end that "it stands to reason" they could meet the matriarch again.

When it came to Wanda's role in VisionQuest, showrunner Terry Matalas shared insight into why she didn't appear during the eight-episode series.

"We had lots of discussions," he told E! News in an exclusive interview ahead of its premiere. "I can't talk too much about the future of the MCU, but Wanda always felt present anyway, and I think especially in that very last scene, that intimate scene with Vision and Ultron."

"Paul is talking about losing her, and it's as if she's in the room with them for a moment," he recalled. "Would an appearance from her take away the journey that he's on and become about that? That was a real question. Also, she can't just be back. There has to be a story behind that."

And he emphasized that they only had "so much real estate to be able to do that," but he was looking forward to seeing what the future held for Wanda.

Meanwhile, Spader, reprising his role from Avengers: Age of Ultron, noted just how valuable her physical absence was in the series.

"Sometimes someone's presence is only magnified by their lack thereof," he told E!. "The void that they leave by not being there makes their presence really so much more.”

“If it were that easy for Vision to be able to even imagine her right there and be able to reach out and not touch her, but to imagine her there, that would dissipate his feeling of loss," he posited. "It would fill the void in an odd way, and the void for this show to work, the void had to be empty."

While fans wait to watch Avengers: Doomsday, keep reading for more MCU shows to add to your queue.

Stars: Elizabeth Olsen, Paul Bettany, Kathryn Hahn, Teyonah Parris, Kat Dennings, Randall Park

The first of the MCU's limited TV shows produced by Marvel for Disney+, WandaVision is set in the aftermath of the final battle in Avengers: Endgame, when the population is restored after the Blip.

Wanda Maximoff (Olsen) lives with her husband Vision (Bettany) in a picturesque suburb, but nothing is quite as it seems. WandaVision leads directly into Doctor Strange: Multiverse of Madness, and Parris will return as Monica in Captain Marvel 2.

Stars: Anthony Mackie, Sebastian Stan, Emily Van Camp, Daniel Bruhl, Erin Kellyman, Wyatt Russellet

A few months after the events of Avengers: Endgame, Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) handed over the Captain America shield to Sam Wilson (Mackie). Sam and Bucky (Stan) wrestle with the legacy of Captain America and the idea of a Black man becoming the iconic hero after Sam's decision to hand the shield over to a museum goes awry.

Stars: Tom Hiddleston, Owen Wilson, Sophia Di Martino, Gugu Mbatha-Raw, Wunmi Mosaku, Sophia Di Martino, Richard E. Grant, Sasha Lane

Loki begins in an alternate timeline, after the events of 2012 in Avengers: Endgame.

The Loki we grew to love (Hiddleston) was killed in Avengers: Infinity War, but when the time heist went a little wrong in Avengers: Endgame, the 2012 version of Loki stole the Space Stone and disappeared. Now, Loki has been brought in by the Time Variance Authority to save the sacred timeline from another Loki variant and ends up on a mission to get to the bottom of the TVA itself.

One of the only shows to be renewed for another season, the second installment follows Loki and Mobius (Wilson) as they try to fix the overloaded Temporal Loom, a machine that contains raw energy to power the Sacred Timelines, as the multiverse continues to branch further.

Stars: Jeffrey Wright, Hayley Atwell, Chadwick Boseman, Josh Brolin, Dominic Cooper, Michael Douglas, Chris Hemsworth, Natalie Portman, Karen Gillan, Tom Hiddleston, Sebastian Stan, Paul Rudd and more.

What If...? is an animated series that explores what would have happened if things had turned out very differently in the MCU. What if Peggy became a super soldier instead of Steve? What if T'Challa became Star Lord? The Watcher (Wright) narrates as he observes the multiverse, and a huge number of MCU stars are lending their voices to the show, including the late Boseman.

Stars: Jeremy Renner, Hailee Steinfeld, Florence Pugh, Vera Farmiga, Fra Fee, Tony Dalton, Zahn McClarmon, Brian d'Arcy James, Alaqua Cox

The series follows Clint Barton (Renner) handing over the mantle of Hawkeye to Kate Bishop (Steinfeld). Pugh will reprise her role as Black Widow's sister from the upcoming Black Widow, and Clint's children will also make appearances.

Stars: Iman Vellani, Aramis Knight, Saagar Shaikh, Rish Shah, Matt Lintz, Zenobia Shroff, Mohan Kapur

Vellani plays Kamala Khan, a 16-year-old Pakistani-American growing up in Jersey City. "A great student, avid gamer, and voracious fan-fic scribe, Kamala has a special affinity for superheroes, particularly Captain Marvel," the Marvel description reads. "However, Kamala struggles to fit in at home and at school—that is, until she gets superpowers like the heroes she's always looked up to. Life is easier with superpowers, right?"

Stars: Tatiana Maslany, Renée Elise Goldsberry, Mark Ruffalo, Tim Roth, Ginger Gonzaga

She-Hulk is a comedy about a lawyer named Jennifer Walters (Maslany) who specializes in cases involving superhumans. She is a cousin of Bruce Banner (Ruffalo) and can also transform into a big, green version of herself. It will consist of 10 episodes.

Stars: Oscar Isaac, Ethan Hawke, May Calamawy

Isaac stars as Marc Spector, a former CIA agent whose life is saved by the Moon God Khonshu.

Stars: Samuel L. Jackson, Ben Mendelsohn, Kingsley Ben-Adir, Olivia Colman, Emilia Clarke

Nick Fury (Jackson) reunites with the Skrull Talos (Mendelsohn), showcasing a faction of shapeshifting Skrulls who have been infiltrating Earth for years. Ben-Adir plays villain Gravik, a ruthless general leading a militia of shapeshifting aliens.

In a series based on a classic Marvel comic, James Rhodes (Cheadle) must confront one of Tony Stark's greatest fears when Stark tech falls into the wrong hands.

Stars: Dominique Thorne, Anthony Ramos, Sacha Baron Cohen

Thorne plays Riri Williams, a genius inventor who creates the most advanced suit of armor since Iron Man.

Stars: Kathryn Hahn, Joe Locke, Aubrey Plaza, Patti LuPone

Three years after being trapped in Westview in WandaVision, powerless witch Agatha Harkness (Hahn) escapes with the help of a mysterious teen (Locke) and must face a new coven of witches.

Stars: Paul Bettany, James Spader, Ruaridh Mollica, Emily Hampshire

After Vision (Bettany) is resurrected as a synth-like version of himself in WandaVision, he tries to understand who he is through various MCU AI personas embedded in his core processor, including Ultron (Spader), E.D.I.T.H. (Hampshire) and F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady). His life goes awry when a bounty is placed on Vision's head, leading him to go on the run with a teen who may or may not be the reincarnation of his son and Wanda Maximoff's son Tommy (Mollica).

#906. Salty grains in Saturn’s outermost ring formed from the slow freeze of plumes from the moon Enceladus

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Kevin P. Hand is at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, California 91109, USA.

Saturn is surrounded by eight rings of ice and rock fragments, with the E ring being the outermost one. Supplied with material mainly by the erupting ice plumes of Enceladus, one of Saturn’s moons, the E ring continues to inform studies of planetary science and astrobiology. Now, nine years after the Cassini spacecraft transmitted its last gasp of data from Saturn back to Earth, Postberg et al.1 report in Science Advances the latest analysis of the grains that make up the E ring. They also discuss what these data can tell us about the subsurface ocean of Enceladus, including whether it could be habitable.

#905. Bone broth, sweets ban and acupuncture: Harry Kane’s road to record England cap

Obsessive attention to detail is helping striker to reach new heights – and a 126th international appearance on Thursday

It was Harry Kane’s dirty little secret. Something the England captain got up to after matches. He felt he deserved the indulgence. Yes, it can be revealed, Kane loved to reward himself after a gruelling 90 minutes with a bag of sweets. “I do like a Haribo,” he said with a smile after the Nations League win against Czechia in Prague at the end of September.

No more. At the beginning of last season, Kane took the decision to cut out the naughty treats. After a while, he noticed a difference. He felt sharper; able to sprint more, make a greater number of accelerations. Was it down to this latest entry on the list of personal sacrifices? Or was it a consequence of his broader health regime, the scope of which is mind-blowing?

The bottom line was that there was a gain. So Kane did what he has always done – he leaned into it. Strongly. As the goals flowed as never before, he said it became “addictive”. The 33-year-old striker finished the season with 61 goals for Bayern Munich and 12 for England. According to data from Gradient Sports, his sprints and accelerations per 90 minutes for Bayern were up significantly on 2024-25. This season, he has 10 goals for Bayern and six for England. Again, his sprint and acceleration statistics have improved.

It is a window into Kane’s mentality, the insatiable quest for self‑improvement, the fixation with details large and small, which was the basis for his Ballon d’Or coronation two weeks ago. It is why, as he prepares to make his 126th England appearance against Croatia at Wembley on Thursday night and overtake Peter Shilton as the nation’s most capped men’s player, it is hard to argue that he is not getting better with age.

Kane is the ultimate modern‑day professional, who controls everything he can control. The no‑sweets choice is the most recent on a dietary journey that started more than 10 years ago when he began to work with the nutritional specialist Dan Sargeant.

Kane had his meals prepared by Sargeant, who believes that everyone has a different reaction to food and analyses everything from bone broths to the white bits on oranges to tailor individual plans. Kane has not worked directly with Sargeant since his transfer from Tottenham to Bayern in 2023 – he has a different chef in Munich – but he continues to follow his advice.

It is common knowledge that Kane is teetotal during the season, albeit he had a few drinks as he celebrated his Ballon d’Or triumph. It was the first and almost certainly the last time he broke his rule. Similarly, everyone is aware of Kane’s obsession with recovery after games; his use of ice baths and infrared saunas. He also places great store in the quality of his sleep.

Less well-known is the depth of his relationship with his private doctor, Alejandro Elorriaga Claraco, who specialises in electrical neurofunctional acupuncture. Kane started seeing the Spaniard on a recommendation from the golfer Justin Rose after sustaining a severe hamstring tear playing for Spurs in 2020.

Claraco is based in Canada but travels to see Kane and spends at least a week every month with him. During that time, he will treat Kane on a table for four to five hours each day, getting his muscles pumping with acupuncture needles hooked up to a small battery. Claraco has been fundamental in helping Kane to understand his body; what he can and cannot do, plus how he gets over injuries.

Kane is hurtling towards his record-breaking England cap. He is in better shape than ever; mentally, as well, because he has grown so much as a leader and public speaker, particularly over the past few years of his England captaincy. He was given the armband on a full-time basis by Gareth Southgate in 2018, the fulfilment of a boyhood dream.

Kane has never hidden the fact that England is his priority, mainly because he was such a fan of the national team as a boy. It will be an emotional occasion for him against Croatia and his journey will flash before him. It began with the goal on his debut against Lithuania in 2015, 79 seconds after he came on as a substitute for Wayne Rooney, and it is worth dwelling on the numbers.

Of Kane’s 91 goals – an England record – 21 have come at major tournaments: 14 at World Cups, seven at European Championships. Only two European players have more combined goals at World Cup tournaments and European Championships: Cristiano Ronaldo (25) and Kylian Mbappé (23). Kane has scored 12 times in the knockout rounds. As an aside, he has 21 assists for England, which puts him joint‑second on the all-time men’s list with Steven Gerrard, behind David Beckham (39).

The best moments? Kane is very fond of the Lithuania goal, not to mention the last-gasp winner against Tunisia in the 2018 World Cup group stage and the clincher against Germany in the last 16 at Euro 2020. He always says that one of his best England performances was against Ukraine in the quarter-final of that tournament, when he scored twice. More recently, there were the two goals that saved the day against the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the last 32 of the World Cup last summer.

Kane’s penalties are a major part of his England story. His record shows 26 successes and five misses, although he scored on the rebound against Denmark in the Euro 2020 semi-final. His conversion against the Netherlands in the Euro 2024 semi-final involved withstanding incredible pressure. Ditto the one against Mexico in the last 16 of this past World Cup. The scar that will never heal was the miss in the 2-1 World Cup quarter-final defeat by France in Qatar in 2022. Was it the low point of his career? Kane is on record as saying the World Cup semi-final exit against Argentina in the summer was worse.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

He was never supposed to make it this far; to reach the Hollywood moment of winning the Ballon d’Or, receiving the trophy from the Brazilian Ronaldo and giving an acceptance speech that tugged hard on the heartstrings. His voice wobbled as he paid tribute to his mother, Kim, who had tears in her eyes, and his father, Pat.

Kane was never a wonderkid at Spurs; he had difficult loans at Norwich and Leicester. He was doubted. It is true to say he has wrung every last drop from his talent; the dedication has underpinned everything. And yet the raw ability was always there, something often overlooked.

Harry Redknapp, the manager who gave Kane his Spurs debut in 2011, tells a story from the player’s formative days. It involved a behind-closed-doors game at the training ground against Birmingham, whose centre‑half Scott Dann was on the verge of a move to Arsenal. Birmingham included Dann in their team as he returned from a minor injury and Arsenal asked Redknapp whether they could come along to watch.

“I got a call from Pat Rice [the Arsenal assistant manager] and Steve Rowley [the chief scout] and I said: ‘Of course, no problem, come over,’” Redknapp said. “Arsenal were signing Scott Dann, they just wanted to check his fitness. So they came to watch and I think Harry scored four goals that day and Arsenal didn’t sign Scott Dann. Harry absolutely ran amok that day.

“We always felt Harry was going to be a player. No one could come here now and say we knew he was going to be England’s all-time record caps holder, record scorer and Ballon d’Or winner. Anyone who says that is talking rubbish. But we did think there was a player there. How good he would be, no one was ever sure.”

Kane was breathtaking when he broke through for Spurs and England in 2014-15 and there were people who thought that would be it; he was tagged as a one-season wonder. He has been a wonder in every season since, the dynamics finessed, perhaps, by the sense that nothing has been given to him; his humility, too.

There has never been the hint of scandal about Kane and it is perfectly possible that Haribos may be his biggest vice. The Ballon d’Or is the Boy Next d’Or and there was genuine happiness in all quarters when he won the award – not only among his friends in the game. That said, the reaction of his former Spurs teammate Son Heung‑min, who is at Los Angeles FC, was gold. He tore off on a goal celebration‑style run at his club’s training ground when he heard the news.

Where can Kane take this? When will it end? Nobody knows but two things are clear. He is equipped to keep pushing for a good number of years and it has long since passed the point where it is reasonable to doubt him.

#904. Vinicius Jr sends message to Sudan boy who received prosthetic legs

Watch: VinÃ­cius Jr's surprise message to boy who received prosthetic legs after Sudan drone strike

In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.

The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger VinÃ­cius JÃºnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.

Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.

We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.

More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.

Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.

More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.

In his video message, Real Madrid star VinÃ­cius Jr invited Zaher to watch a Real Madrid match together

The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.

For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.

When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was VinÃ­cius JÃºnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together.

"I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.

VinÃ­cius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."

Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."

Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new VinÃ­cius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer.

"Tell VinÃ­cius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".

Zaher is one of millions of children whose lives have been devastated by Sudan's civil war

Zaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF.

Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets.

Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck.

"I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year.

She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer."

Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes.

Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection.

"I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to," he said at the time.

There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world.

Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising Â£45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care.

Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war.

Zaher has learned to use his new legs with months of support from doctors and physiotherapists in Cairo

After months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged.

For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive.

'I can't afford to save both twins': Sudan's war left one mother with an impossible choice

A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan

Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through.

"He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself."

His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them.

As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him.

He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home.

For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war.

Khartoum has suffered extensive damage, with many buildings damaged and their contents stolen

The state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted.

Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states. The group also warned of "potential famine".

"I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries.

Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows.

Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs.

Additional reporting by Scarlett Barter and Abdelrahman Abutaleb
